# Worsening Wheezing and Falling Oxygen After a New Rescue Inhaler: What the Evidence Says

**Short answer: No, this is not your body "adjusting." What you're describing — gasping worse within minutes of using a rescue inhaler, with oxygen saturation dropping into the low 90s — is the textbook clinical picture of a known, FDA-labeled, potentially life-threatening adverse reaction called *paradoxical bronchospasm*. Every manufacturer's label for this drug class instructs patients to stop the inhaler immediately and get alternative therapy. You should not wait this out, and you should not simply stop and have nothing to fall back on — you need to contact a clinician or pharmacist today, and given the 91% readings, an urgent evaluation is warranted. I'm not a clinician and this isn't a diagnosis, but the direction of the evidence here is unusually unambiguous.**

---

## 1. What you're describing has a name, and it's in the label

Paradoxical bronchospasm is constriction of the airway muscle that happens when you expected the opposite — the inhaler is supposed to open your airways, and instead it tightens them. The DailyMed prescribing information for albuterol sulfate HFA is explicit:

> "Albuterol Sulfate HFA Inhalation Aerosol can produce paradoxical bronchospasm that may be life threatening. If paradoxical bronchospasm occurs, Albuterol Sulfate HFA Inhalation Aerosol should be discontinued immediately and alternative therapy instituted. It should be recognized that paradoxical bronchospasm, when associated with inhaled formulations, frequently occurs with the first use of a new canister."
> — https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=7bb5b6dd-9105-4ee7-b205-ed79cf4b371b

The same language appears across the entire albuterol class — Ventolin HFA, ProAir HFA, generic albuterol HFA, and albuterol inhalation solution:

- ProAir HFA label (FDA): "Life-threatening paradoxical bronchospasm may occur. Discontinue PROAIR HFA immediately and treat with alternative therapy." — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2019/021457s036lbl.pdf
- Ventolin HFA label (FDA): same warning — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2014/020983s032lbl.pdf
- Albuterol inhalation solution label (FDA): "as with other inhaled beta-adrenergic agonists, albuterol sulfate inhalation solution can produce paradoxical bronchospasm, which may be life threatening. If paradoxical bronchospasm occurs, albuterol sulfate inhalation solution should be discontinued immediately and alternative therapy instituted." — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/020949Orig1s027lbl.pdf

The patient-facing version of that same label is even plainer: *"worsening trouble breathing, coughing, and wheezing (paradoxical bronchospasm). If this happens, stop using Albuterol Sulfate Inhalation Aerosol and call your healthcare provider or get emergency help right away."* — https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=fd0389e0-3713-42e0-8ef2-3bb97676fded

Three features of your account line up precisely with that description: the worsening is **(a) immediate (within minutes), (b) in the wrong direction (worse, not better), and (c) tied to a new inhaler.** Cleveland Clinic's patient-facing summary states the same: "In rare cases, bronchospasm medications like albuterol can actually make your symptoms worse. This is a paradoxical bronchospasm. If this happens, stop using your bronchodilator immediately and tell your healthcare provider." — https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22620-bronchospasm

## 2. How common is this? Not as rare as you'd hope

Published real-world data puts it well above "vanishingly rare."

A study of 4,593 patients who underwent pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry at a large academic medical center found:

- **201 patients (4.4%)** showed *significant bronchoconstriction* after albuterol
- 849 patients (18.5%) showed the expected bronchodilation
- 3,543 patients (77.1%) showed no significant change
- No significant relationship with sex, race/ethnicity, or BMI

Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/326093696_Prevalence_of_paradoxical_bronchoconstriction_after_inhaled_albuterol

**Quantitative check:** 201 ÷ 4,593 = 0.04377 → **4.4%**, or roughly **1 in 23 patients**. The three groups sum to 100.0% (4.4 + 18.5 + 77.1). This means the "expected" response — your breathing actually improving — is not the majority outcome in that cohort either.

A peer-reviewed case report in the *American Journal of Case Reports* notes the phenomenon "occurring in up to 8% of patients," and emphasizes it is "an under-recognized adverse event" that is documented on package inserts. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6192384/

So there are two independent estimates: ~4.4% in a large spirometry cohort, and "up to 8%" cited in the case-report literature. Either way, this is a recognized, non-trivial reaction — not a fringe curiosity, and not something to be dismissed as adjustment.

That same case report is worth reading in full because the patient's story mirrors yours almost exactly: a 25-year-old with moderate asthma who reported "recurrent episodes of acute shortness of breath **immediately following each administration of albuterol for 4 weeks**." His spirometry confirmed it objectively — FEV₁ (a standard lung-function measure) *fell* after albuterol. The reported percentage-point changes in percent-predicted FEV₁ were:

| Inhaler given | Pre → post FEV₁ (L) | % predicted | Change (percentage points) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Levalbuterol HFA (Xopenex) | 2.19 → 1.70 | 50% → 29% | **−21** |
| Albuterol HFA (ProAir) | 2.68 → 2.25 | 68% → 57% | **−11** |
| Nebulized albuterol sulfate | 2.68 → 3.04 | 68% → 77% | **+9** |
| Ipratropium HFA (Atrovent) | 2.47 → 2.73 | 62% → 69% | **+7** |

Note the direction: the two *metered-dose inhalers* made his lungs measurably worse, while the nebulized form and an anticholinergic made them better. He was switched to an ipratropium rescue inhaler and had no further symptoms. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6192384/

The proposed mechanism is the **inactive ingredients (excipients)**, not the albuterol molecule itself. Oleic acid (an excipient in Xopenex HFA) and ethanol (an excipient in ProAir HFA) are specifically implicated as triggers of airway hyperresponsiveness in people with allergically inflamed airways. This is why the nebulized form — which lacks those excipients — did not cause the same reaction.

## 3. Your oxygen readings: 91% is not a "watch and wait" number

Your saturation dropped from your usual ~95% to 91%. That is a **4-percentage-point fall**, and it matters because **91% sits below the 92% threshold** that major guidelines use to flag severe or life-threatening asthma.

**Quantitative check:** 91% < 92% → the reading falls on the severe side of the guideline cutoff, not the "probably fine" side.

How the thresholds break down:

- **NICE (UK)** lists "oxygen saturation less than 92%" among the features of a **severe or life-threatening asthma attack** requiring emergency assessment, and says to give oxygen and continuously monitor anyone at 94% or less while waiting for transfer. — https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/breathlessness/management/management/
- **Asthma + Lung UK** lists "oxygen saturation of less than 92%" under the heading **"Signs of a life-threatening asthma attack"** — alongside confusion, exhaustion, cyanosis, and silent chest — with the instruction to call an ambulance. — https://www.asthmaandlung.org.uk/healthcare-professionals/adult-asthma/uncontrolled
- **GINA 2026** (the international asthma guideline) classifies a severe presentation as including **oxygen saturation less than 92%**, and notes that values below 90% are "especially concerning." — https://www.jucm.com/urgent-care-textbook-wheezing-and-asthma/
- A clinical textbook chapter summarizing GINA 2026 lists "oxygen saturation <92% on room air" among the triggers for **immediate ED transfer/EMS**. — same source

So by guideline criteria, a reproducible dip to 91% accompanied by worsening breathlessness is a severe feature — regardless of what you conclude about the inhaler.

## 4. Important caveat: don't over-trust the home oximeter — but don't ignore it either

You should know the limits of your device, because it cuts in *both* directions.

- **The FDA** has issued a formal safety communication that pulse oximeters "have limitations and a risk of inaccuracy under certain circumstances," and states: "Do not rely only on a pulse oximeter... it also is important to keep track of your symptoms or how you feel." Factors affecting accuracy include poor circulation, skin pigmentation, skin thickness, skin temperature, current tobacco use, and fingernail polish. — https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/products-and-medical-procedures/pulse-oximeters and https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USFDA/bulletins/2c276cb
- **A Cochrane review** specifically on home pulse oximetry in asthma found "no studies and no evidence to support or refute the use of home pulse oximetry in self management of asthma," and advised that "people should not use a pulse oximeter without seeking advice from a qualified healthcare professional." — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9426972/ and https://www.cochrane.org/CD011584/AIRWAYS_pulse-oximeters-used-self-monitor-oxygen-saturation-levels-part-personalised-asthma-action-plan
- **On skin tone bias**, a large BMJ study of 11,018 paired SpO₂–SaO₂ measurements found all tested oximeters **overestimated at lower values and underestimated at higher values** of true saturation, and that readings averaged **0.6–1.5 percentage points higher** in patients with darker skin tone. The false-negative rate — a reassuring SpO₂ reading despite genuinely low arterial oxygen — was **2.3- to 7.1-fold higher** in darker-skinned patients. — https://www.bmj.com/content/392/bmj-2025-085535

**Why this cuts both ways:** if your oximeter is biased toward *over*-reading at low saturations (which is the documented pattern), your true saturation could be **worse than 91%**, not better. And the FDA's own framing tells you the reading should be interpreted *alongside* symptoms — which in your case are actively worsening. Here the device and the symptoms agree, which is the scenario where you act.

The critical point: **the symptom is the primary signal. The oximeter is corroboration, not the decision-maker.**

## 5. Other explanations worth ruling out (the ones a clinician would check)

You said the pharmacist showed you the technique and you're "pretty sure" it's right. That's good, but technique is only one variable. Other possibilities that produce a similar "new inhaler, worse symptoms" picture:

**a) A formulation or generic switch.** Generic inhaled drugs are therapeutically equivalent but "may differ in their formulation and inhalation device." Inhaler devices vary markedly in design, operation, and drug delivery to the lungs, and switching device "may be associated with a poor inhalation technique, reduced disease control and quality of life, increased use of other treatments and health care resources." — https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1517/17425247.2013.852182 and https://karger.com/res/article-abstract/88/4/346/308097/The-Importance-of-Continuity-in-Inhaler-Device

Notably, the FDA has previously deemed albuterol HFA formulations **not** biologically equivalent to one another, and pharmacists cannot legally substitute between them — meaning the specific product you got matters. — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1555415509001962

**b) Excipient sensitivity.** As above, ethanol and oleic acid are documented culprits. Different brands contain different excipients. Ventolin HFA, for instance, contains albuterol sulfate in propellant HFA-134a and **no other excipients**, whereas ProAir HFA contains ethanol. — https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=d92c5d6b-ff10-4087-36a2-1cfc464cb967

**c) A different drug entirely.** If your new blue inhaler is a *dual-action* rescue inhaler — e.g., AIRSUPRA (albuterol/budesonide) — that's a different product with its own label. Its actuator is white, not blue, so it's probably not what you have, but worth confirming what you were actually dispensed. — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/214070s001lblCorrected.pdf

**d) A device fault or delivery failure.** If the device isn't delivering drug, you'd feel worse from *untreated* asthma. There are real precedents in this exact product category:
- **AIRSUPRA recall (May 2025, AstraZeneca):** a limited voluntary recall of sample lots because up to 0.005% of a lot could contain units "in which the actuator mouthpiece is in the incorrect orientation resulting in **non-delivery of dose**." The recall notice flagged that the risk "would be high if an acute severe asthma [attack occurred]." — https://www.ipdpharma.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/AstraZeneca-Airsupra-Recall-5.22.2025.pdf
- **Cipla albuterol sulfate inhalation aerosol recall (Class III, announced August 2025):** 20,352 packs, lot **4IB0519**, expiration **April 30, 2026**, recalled after stability testing failed particle-size-distribution specs at the 12-month mark. Class III means adverse health consequences are unlikely, but the lot was pulled. — https://www.hmpgloballearningnetwork.com/site/pln/news/class-iii-recall-albuterol-sulfate-inhalation-aerosol
- **Nephron albuterol inhalation *solution* recall (Class II, initiated March 2026, published April 2026):** 146,280 vials, lot **AB6001**, exp **1/15/2027**, for illegible labeling — this is nebulizer solution, not an MDI, so probably not your product. — https://plainrecalls.com/recall/d-0479-2026-albuterol-sulfate-inhalation-solution-0-5-25-mg-5-ml-5-mg-ml-30x5-ml-ster

**Actionable:** check the lot number and expiration date printed on your canister against these. Also confirm the inhaler was **primed** before first use — the AIRSUPRA label, like other MDIs, requires priming prior to first use and re-priming if unused for more than 7 days. — https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=e60aa9f9-5139-44df-b886-ebddc3c7eb13

**e) Plain old worsening asthma — which is itself serious.** The albuterol label warns: "If the patient needs more doses of albuterol... than usual, this may be a marker of destabilization of asthma and requires re-evaluation of the patient and the treatment regimen, giving special consideration of the possible need for anti-inflammatory treatment (e.g., corticosteroids)." — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/020949Orig1s027lbl.pdf

This matters because modern guidance has moved away from albuterol-only rescue. **GINA 2026** states that "all adults, adolescents and children aged 6–11 years should receive treatment that includes ICS" (inhaled corticosteroids), and that for adults and adolescents, **anti-inflammatory reliever treatment with combination ICS-formoterol is the preferred treatment** — because it reduces severe attacks and requires only one inhaler. — https://ginasthma.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/GINA-Summary-Guide-2026-WEB-WMS.pdf

The UK's MHRA drug-safety update put it bluntly: "excessive use of SABA to relieve acute asthma symptoms may mask progression of the underlying disease and contribute to an increased risk of severe and potentially life-threatening asthma exacerbations." The MHRA also confirmed an association "across all asthma severities between having 3 or more SABA prescriptions over the 1-year study period and experiencing severe asthma exacerbations," independent of other maintenance therapy. — https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/short-acting-beta-2-agonists-saba-salbutamol-and-terbutaline-reminder-of-the-risks-from-overuse-in-asthma-and-to-be-aware-of-changes-in-the-saba-prescribing-guidelines

**The quantitative case against leaning harder on a rescue inhaler that's making things worse:**

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis (27 studies) found that SABA overuse (≥3 canisters/year) was associated with:
- **Significantly higher mortality:** RR = **2.04** (95% CI 1.37–3.04, p < 0.001)
- **Significantly more acute exacerbations:** RR = **1.93** (95% CI 1.24–3.03, p < 0.001)

— https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12186600/

A Swedish nationwide cohort of **365,324** asthma patients (the SABINA programme) found dose-dependent risk escalation:

| SABA canisters/year | Exacerbation HR (95% CI) | Mortality HR (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|
| 3–5 | 1.26 (1.24–1.28) | 1.26 (1.14–1.39) |
| 6–10 | 1.44 (1.41–1.46) | 1.67 (1.49–1.87) |
| ≥11 | 1.77 (1.72–1.83) | **2.35** |

30% of that cohort overused SABA. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31949111/

**The implication for your situation:** the instinct to "use it more to push through" is exactly the wrong move. It's the behavior most strongly associated with bad outcomes, and if this inhaler is actively bronchoconstricting you, more puffs means more provocation, not more relief.

## 6. A note on the "is it just in my head?" question

You may be wondering whether you're imagining it. There's a genuinely relevant study here — but it argues that your *symptoms* are more reliable than your *attribution*.

Researchers gave 48 patients with airflow limitation their usual brand of salbutamol MDI for one week, then a "new" MDI for a week — **but the "new" inhaler was literally the same brand, disguised with a different label.** Results:
- 46% thought the "new" MDI was *better*
- 27% thought it was *worse*
- 27% perceived no difference
- 70% expressed a preference for one over the other — despite zero actual difference

— https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1057/palgrave.jgm.4940070

This is a real caution against assuming any *change* is a *harm*. **But it does not apply cleanly to you**, for three reasons: (1) your reaction is immediate and reproducible rather than a vague preference; (2) it's accompanied by an objective measurement — the oximeter — that is moving in the same direction; and (3) the reaction you describe matches a labeled, documented, mechanistically plausible adverse event with a known prevalence. Perception studies explain why *some* switches feel bad; they don't explain why a specific inhaler reliably drives your saturation down within minutes.

## 7. What to do

**Right now:**
1. **Stop using this specific inhaler.** This is what the manufacturer's own label instructs. Do not take another dose to "test" it. Do not increase your dose hoping to push through.
2. **Do not stop and stay silent.** You need a replacement rescue plan today — you should not be left with no way to treat an attack. You need a clinician or pharmacist to swap you to something else (see options below).
3. **Contact your prescriber or pharmacist today** — same day, not next week. Tell them the specific words: *"worsening wheeze and chest tightness within minutes of using this inhaler, plus my home oxygen readings have dropped from ~95% to 91% since I started it three weeks ago."* Name the product, the lot number, and the date you started it.
4. **Seek emergency care (call 911 / go to the ER) now** if any of the following are true: you can't speak in full sentences or walk without stopping for breath; your lips, fingertips, or nail beds look blue, pale, or gray; you feel drowsy, confused, or exhausted; your chest goes quiet when you'd expect wheezing (reduced air movement is *worse* than audible wheeze, not better); or your symptoms worsen further. — https://www.cdc.gov/asthma/action-plan/documents/asthma-action-plan-508.pdf and https://healthy.kaiserpermanente.org/health-wellness/health-encyclopedia/he.asthma-action-plan-red-zone.hw161511

The CDC asthma action plan is explicit about the red-zone logic: if you're still in the red zone after taking your quick-relief medicine and 15 minutes have passed without reaching your doctor, **go to the hospital or call 911**. — https://www.cdc.gov/asthma/action-plan/documents/asthma-action-plan-508.pdf

Given that your "quick-relief medicine" is the thing apparently making you worse, that 15-minute clock is effectively already expired.

**When you speak to a clinician, raise these specific points:**
- Ask them to verify the **exact product, brand, and lot number** you were dispensed, and whether it's a change from what you used before.
- Ask whether you've been switched between formulations with different excipients (ethanol, oleic acid) or to a different propellant/device.
- Ask about a **trial of an alternative rescue agent.** The case-report literature shows patients like this can be successfully managed with alternatives — the documented example was an ipratropium (anticholinergic) rescue inhaler, plus nebulized albuterol for the acute setting. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6192384/
- Ask whether your **controller (anti-inflammatory) therapy** needs to be stepped up. GINA 2026 no longer supports SABA-only treatment for anyone. — https://ginasthma.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/GINA-Summary-Guide-2026-WEB-WMS.pdf
- If there's genuine uncertainty about whether it's the drug or your asthma worsening, **pre/post-bronchodilator spirometry** is the objective test that sorted it out in the published case. That's a clinic-based test; it's the right tool for this question.
- Ask about a **written asthma action plan** with explicit zones. You have a home oximeter but — per the Cochrane review — no evidence supports home oximetry in asthma self-management *unless* it's embedded in a personalized action plan with a clear protocol. Right now you have the device without the protocol. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9426972/

**Do not:**
- Do not "wait for your body to adjust." There is no adjustment phase in the labeling for this reaction. The label says discontinue, not taper or persist.
- Do not take extra puffs to compensate. SABA overuse is independently associated with a doubling of mortality risk (RR 2.04).
- Do not rely on the oximeter alone to decide whether to seek care. The FDA warns against this, and the device may be *under*-reading your danger at low saturations. Use symptoms as the primary trigger.

## 8. Uncertainty and limits of this assessment

I want to be straight about what I can't determine from here:

1. **I don't know exactly what you were dispensed.** "Blue rescue inhaler" is most consistent with Ventolin HFA ("a blue plastic inhaler with a blue cap") or a blue generic albuterol HFA. ProAir HFA uses a **red** actuator and Proventil a yellow/orange one; AIRSUPRA uses a **white** actuator. — https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=d92c5d6b-ff10-4087-36a2-1cfc464cb967, https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=133fb50a-68d3-4d1b-a47a-67d07cc48da5, https://www.healthline.com/health/asthma/inhaler-colors Color coding is convention, not regulation, so this is inference, not identification.
2. **I can't distinguish paradoxical bronchospasm from worsening underlying asthma** from your description alone. Both produce worsening breathlessness on a new inhaler. The distinguishing features — immediate timing tied tightly to each dose, and reproducibility — point toward the former, and that's why spirometry exists.
3. **Your home oximeter is not a medical-grade device.** The FDA notes medical-grade oximeters must be accurate within 3% of measured saturation, while consumer devices "are not subject to the same approval rigor." — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11108103/ Your 91% may be off by a few points in either direction. That uncertainty is an argument for acting sooner, not later, because the documented bias at low saturations runs toward false reassurance.
4. **The prevalence estimates come from different populations.** The 4.4% figure comes from patients referred for spirometry — a selected group that may not represent all inhaler users. The "up to 8%" figure is cited in a case report referencing a product label. Both are imperfect, but both establish that this is a recognized, non-rare event.
5. **I did not find evidence of an HFA-152a propellant rollout causing this.** GSK announced positive Phase III data (October 2025) for a low-carbon Ventolin using HFA-152a, with launch *expected from 2026* — but the data showed therapeutic equivalence and comparable safety to the current HFA-134a propellant, and no serious treatment-related adverse events were reported. — https://www.gsk.com/en-gb/media/press-releases/gsk-announces-positive-pivotal-phase-iii-data-for-next-generation-low-carbon-version-of-ventolin-salbutamol-metered-dose-inhaler/ and https://nutrition-evidence.com/article/559370/developing-low-carbon-salbutamol-mdi-assessment-of-relative-bioavailability-and-pharmacodynamic-relative-potency-of-salbutamol-mdi-with-propellant-hfa-152a

   That said, history is instructive: when MDIs transitioned from CFC to HFA propellants in the early 2000s, "differences in taste and feel hampered a seamless patient transition." — https://exa.ai/library/publication/s0hn664qpc5 So *any* propellant or formulation change can produce a rough transition even when equivalence is formally demonstrated.

---

## Bottom line

Your instinct that something is wrong is correct, and the specific pattern you've described — worse within minutes, on a new inhaler, with oxygen falling below 92% — is not "adjustment." # How Evert Calderon Is Using SuperMoney and Novae at Mesa Group Consulting

## Summary answer

Evert Calderon is not just "mentioning" SuperMoney — Mesa Group Consulting's own legal disclosure and partner page confirm that **SuperMoney and Novae are both commissioned affiliate/fulfillment partners of his business**, and the Miro board pages map exactly onto the product catalogs of those two platforms. The cleanest reading is:

- **SuperMoney** is the *affiliate referral engine* for consumer lending pages (credit cards, personal loans, auto refi, student loan refi, debt consolidation). Mesa routes site visitors to SuperMoney comparison pages through tracked links and earns a commission when users take a product.
- **Novae** is the *fulfillment/co-brand backend* for Mesa's protection and business pages (debt relief, trust & will, life insurance, business debt relief, business credit) — the on-page applications and lead forms are provided by Novae's "Co-Brand" turnkey program, and Mesa earns per-signup and per-funding commissions.

The Miro board is a page-architecture plan: each new page on mesagroupconsulting.com is explicitly assigned to whichever affiliate backend (SuperMoney or Novae) supplies that page's offers, forms, and commission structure.

---

## 1. Evert Calderon and Mesa Group Consulting

Mesa Group Consulting is a credit-repair / financial-consulting firm in Bakersfield, CA. Evert Calderon is listed on the company site as **"Senior Writer & Spokesperson"**, with a stated background "across banking, financial consulting, and credit education" (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/author/evert-calderon). He is also registered with the Credit Consultants Association as a board-certified consultant under Mesa Group Consulting (https://ccasite.org/members/find-a-list-consultants/name/evert-calderon/). The user describes him as owner/operator; the public site frames him as the public face, while the site's founder story (419 credit score, immigrant parents) is told in first-person-adjacent language but does not explicitly name him.

The business model on the site is explicit: core credit repair/consulting services **plus** a "Mesa Marketplace" of lending, debt, insurance, and estate-planning products routed to third-party partners. The site's own footer and disclosures state: "We may receive compensation through affiliate partnerships and referral arrangements" (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure).

---

## 2. SuperMoney: what it is and why it maps to the Miro board

SuperMoney is an independent financial product comparison marketplace (operating since 2013, 2M+ registered members, 50+ product verticals, Inc. 5000 2022–2025, SOC 2 Type II certified). It makes money three ways: commissions from financial institutions when users take a product through the site, a paid app subscription, and advertising (https://help.supermoney.com/article/62-how-does-supermoney-make-money).

Critically for Mesa, SuperMoney runs a **publisher affiliate program** ("Monetize") with three products:
- **Super Links** — tracked referral links placed in a publisher's content; the publisher earns commission when users complete offers on SuperMoney's comparison pages, with "co-branded pages" that monetize even when the specific product written about doesn't pay out.
- **Money Marketplace** — an embedded comparison experience inside the publisher's own site, under the publisher's brand.
- **Pre-qualification Platform** — real-time loan pre-qualification on the publisher's site (https://help.supermoney.com/article/33-how-can-i-partner-with-supermoney; https://www.supermoney.com/monetize).

Commission rates are not published by SuperMoney itself, but third-party affiliate-network listings report **up to 30% per sale**, available through networks such as Impact, ShareASale, Rakuten, Awin, and Takeads (https://takeads.com/merchants/supermoney-us/; https://affsignal.com/merchant/Supermoney).

The five Miro board items tagged "supermoney affiliate" — **credit cards, personal loans, auto loan refi, student loan refi, debt consolidation** — are precisely SuperMoney's comparison verticals. SuperMoney's own affiliate pitch literally lists "banking to credit cards to debt to taxes," and its knowledge base confirms it covers "credit cards, debt help, insurance, investment, loans, mortgage, personal finance, refinance" (https://help.supermoney.com/article/33-how-can-i-partner-with-supermoney). Mesa Group's Affiliate Disclosure confirms the relationship in plain terms:

> "SuperMoney: Financial product comparison platform offering personal loans, auto loan refinancing, student loan refinancing, debt consolidation loans, and credit card comparisons. When you use SuperMoney through our referral links or secure loans/products, we may receive a commission."
> — https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure

So for those five pages, Evert is almost certainly using **Super Links or the Money Marketplace embed**: the visitor lands on a Mesa page, clicks through to SuperMoney's comparison tool (or an embedded widget), and Mesa earns a commission on any loan/card originated. This requires no lender licenses, no underwriting infrastructure, and no inventory — Mesa is monetizing its traffic and its clients' shopping intent.

---

## 3. Novae: what it actually is

Novae (Novae, LLC; "Novae Money") is a **fintech direct-selling / MLM company** based in Conyers, Georgia (1506 Klondike Road Ste 403), founded in 2014 by Reco McDaniel (now publicly using "Reco McCambry"). It is a member of the Direct Selling Association (https://novaemoney.com/base/compensation-plan). BehindMLM's independent review summarizes it as a financial services MLM with a 16-rank compensation plan, monthly membership fees, recruitment requirements starting at rank two, team overrides, and residual commissions paid across 10 levels (https://behindmlm.com/mlm-reviews/novae-money-review-financial-services-rebrand-stock-fraud/). Independent reviews note it is "largely a commission aggregator, not a provider" — most services are third-party referrals (https://jessesingh.org/novae-money-review/).

Its consumer and business catalog matches the Miro board almost exactly:
- **Consumer**: debt help, credit cards, personal loans, life insurance (via Policygenius), Will & Trust estate plans, savings accounts, auto refi, student loan refi, credit monitoring, disputes manager.
- **Small business**: business credit, business funding, business debt help, LLC formation, consumer financing, grants.
- **Entrepreneurship**: affiliate program, co-brand program, white-label program.

(https://novaemoney.com/cobrand-program/; https://behindmlm.com/mlm-reviews/novae-money-review-financial-services-rebrand-stock-fraud/)

Key Novae commission figures (from its published compensation plan, compiled by BehindMLM):
- Personal Loans, Business Funding, Consumer Financial Products: **35% of third-party commission**
- Business Credit Finance Suite: **$500/signup** ($200 DIY)
- Life Insurance: **$50/signup**; Will & Trust: **$20–$50/signup**
- Credit/disputes monitoring: **$100/signup**
- Debt Help (consumer): **1% per signup**; Business Debt Help: **50% per signup**
- Co-Brand program: **$500–$900 per signup**; White Label: **$3,000 per signup**
- Affiliate membership: **$349 upfront + $99/month**; ranking unlocks monthly team commissions up to $110,000/mo at the top rank; average participant earned **$1,408 in 2023** per the company's own disclosure.

Novae's "Co-Brand" product is the key link to Mesa. Novae pitches it as a turnkey, branded financial services website: "Earn Commissions Immediately... start offering all of the following in-demand financial services, provided by Novae's industry-leading partners," with "**19 Tailored Sales Pages**" and "**20+ Embedded Forms, Applications and Lead Magnets**" (https://novaemoney.com/cobrand-program/). Mesa Group's own partners page confirms Novae plays exactly this role:

> "Novae powers some of Mesa's most impactful programs: business funding in all 50 states, debt relief for individuals and businesses, and a structured business credit-building program. When clients are ready to step into their financial potential, Novae is the infrastructure that makes it possible."
> — https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/our-partners

Mesa's Affiliate Disclosure likewise names Novae for "Business funding and debt relief services (business and personal)" and discloses: "Mesa Group receives a commission when you secure funding or enroll in debt relief services through Novae" (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure).

---

## 4. The Miro board explained page by page

| Miro board item | Label | What's actually happening |
|---|---|---|
| Credit cards | supermoney affiliate | Mesa page with SuperMoney comparison embed/link; commission on card origination |
| Personal loans | supermoney affiliate | Same mechanism; SuperMoney pre-qualification / loan matching |
| Auto loan refi | supermoney affiliate | SuperMoney vertical |
| Student loan refi | supermoney affiliate | SuperMoney vertical |
| Debt consolidation loan | supermoney affiliate | SuperMoney vertical |
| Debt relief | novae | Novae's consumer debt-help program (1% commission per signup; partner network) |
| Trust & will plan | novae | Novae's Will ($199/$299 retail) and Trust ($499/$599 retail) estate-plan products |
| Life insurance | novae | Novae's Policygenius-powered life insurance funnel ($50/signup commission) |
| Business debt relief | novae | Novae's business debt-help program (50% commission per signup) |
| Business credit | novae | Novae's Business Credit Finance Suite ($995–$2,495 retail; $200–$500/signup commission) |

The five "novae" pages correspond exactly to Novae's published product line, and the five "supermoney" pages correspond exactly to SuperMoney's comparison verticals. The Miro board is a build checklist: Evert assigning each new Mesa page to the affiliate backend that will supply its offers, forms, and revenue share. Notably, Mesa's disclosure separately lists PolicyGenius and Trust & Will as named partners, but on the Miro board they're tagged "novae" — because Novae's co-brand package bundles access to the Policygenius and estate-plan funnels under Novae's contract (https://novaemoney.com/cobrand-program/). The consumer lending pages go to SuperMoney because SuperMoney has the better comparison/pre-qualification technology; the protection and business pages go to Novae because that's where those specific turnkey sales pages and lead forms come from.

---

## 5. The overall business model Evert is building

The evidence describes a three-layer revenue architecture:

1. **Core service layer (owned)** — Mesa's CROA-compliant credit repair and consulting, plus trilingual (English/Spanish/Punjabi) financial coaching. This is the client-acquisition engine and trust layer.
2. **Subscription/affiliate layer (SmartCredit and SuperMoney)** — SmartCredit for credit monitoring (recurring residual commission per enrolled member) and SuperMoney for consumer lending comparisons (one-time or origination-based commissions on cards/loans/refis). Both are mainstream affiliate arrangements; SuperMoney additionally lets Mesa embed the marketplace under its own brand (https://www.supermoney.com/monetize).
3. **High-ticket fulfillment layer (Novae co-brand)** — Novae supplies the infrastructure, sales pages, and applications for the protection (insurance, wills/trusts) and business (funding, business credit, business debt relief) products. Mesa pays for or partners via Novae's co-brand program ($2,499–$4,499) or white-label tier ($24,995) and earns per-signup / percentage commissions (https://novaemoney.com/cobrand-program/; https://behindmlm.com/mlm-reviews/novae-money-review-financial-services-rebrand-stock-fraud/).

So Evert is not "using" SuperMoney to find products to sell — he is using SuperMoney as an **affiliate monetization channel** (traffic → comparison → commission) and Novae as a **white-label/co-brand fulfillment platform** (his own branded product pages powered by Novae's applications). The Miro board is the execution plan for converting Mesa's homepage menu into dedicated, conversion-optimized landing pages, each wired to its respective commission backend. The "Mesa Marketplace" section already visible on the Mesa homepage (credit cards, personal loans, auto refi, student loan refi, debt consolidation, debt relief, trust & will, life insurance) is the live version of that plan (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/for-consumers/credit-cards).

---

## 6. Caveats, risks, and uncertainty

- **Commission amounts are unverifiable.** Mesa explicitly states specific compensation amounts "are confidential and subject to non-disclosure agreements" (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure). SuperMoney's up-to-30% figure comes from third-party network listings; Novae's figures come from its published compensation plan as compiled by BehindMLM. The exact contract between Mesa and each partner is unknown.
- **Novae's reputation is mixed and materially riskier than SuperMoney's.** BehindMLM flags Novae's unregistered share offers ("company stock" for top rank) as likely illegal under SEC rules, notes founder Reco McDaniel's prior association with the collapsed WakeUpNow scheme, and calls the compensation plan recruitment-incentivized (recruiting begins at rank two; the deepest concern is whether most "customers" are actually recruited affiliates) (https://behindmlm.com/mlm-reviews/novae-money-review-financial-services-rebrand-stock-fraud/). The BBB's DSSRC opened monitoring case #231-2025 over income claims made by Novae's salesforce (https://bbbprograms.org/programs/advertising/dssrc/cases/novae). Consumer reviews are mixed (ComplaintsBoard shows a 3.9-star average with complaints about service responsiveness and refunds) (https://www.complaintsboard.com/novae-b144702). None of this means Mesa's arrangement is improper, but it's a materially different risk profile from SuperMoney's (a mainstream comparison site with institutional certifications).
- **The Miro board itself was not directly accessed.** The mapping above rests on the user's description plus exact corroboration from Mesa's public pages (partner page, affiliate disclosure, site menu) and the two companies' own catalogs. The match is very strong, but commission amounts and contract terms remain inferential.
- **Evert's exact title/ownership.** The user says he's owner/operator; public pages title him "Senior Writer & Spokesperson." His CCA listing and the site's constant first-person founder framing suggest he is at minimum the principal and public face; I cannot independently verify corporate ownership (the affiliate disclosure names the legal entity "MESA & CO CONSULTING LLC, dba Mesa Group Consulting").

**Bottom line:** Evert Calderon is using SuperMoney as his commissioned comparison/lead-generation layer for consumer lending products, and Novae as his co-branded fulfillment/lead-generation layer for protection and business products. The Miro board is his roadmap for adding ten new commission-bearing pages to mesagroupconsulting.com — each tagged with the affiliate backend that supplies its offers, forms, and revenue. # Maternal and Perinatal Health in Two Protracted Refugee Settings: Rohingya Camps (Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh) and Karen Camps (Mae La, Thailand), 2017–2023

**A source-grounded comparative analysis, with explicit treatment of three premises that the evidence does not support**

---

## 1. Headline findings

1. **The outcome gap is real and large, but narrower in maternal mortality than in neonatal mortality.** Best-available maternal mortality ratio (MMR) estimates for Rohingya camps cluster at **179/100,000** (prospective-linked RAMOS, Sep 2017–Aug 2018) rising to **~200–450/100,000** in 2021–2023 depending on the live-birth denominator used (worked below). Comparable Karen-side figures are **79/100,000** (SMRU displaced-person camps, 2006–2010) and **126.5/100,000** (Mae Ra Ma Luang + Mae La Oon camps, 2000–2018). Neonatal mortality, by contrast, separates cleanly: **27.0/1,000** live births in Rohingya camps (95% CI 22.3–31.8, Sep 2017–Dec 2018) versus **6–8/1,000** reported in Mae La's UNHCR site reports for 2017–2018 — a **3.4–4.5× gap**.

2. **Skilled birth attendance is the single most divergent indicator.** Mae La reported **96% (2017)** and **95% (2018)**, both above the ≥90% Sphere/UNHCR standard. Cox's Bazar ran roughly **12–30% home delivery in 2018**, improving to a **67% facility delivery rate by June 2021** and **73% by mid-2022** — i.e., a **28–29 percentage-point SBA gap** persisting at the end of the study window.

3. **A true postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) incidence comparison cannot be constructed from available evidence.** Cox's Bazar data report PPH as a **cause fraction of maternal deaths** (28% in 2017–18, 29.2% in 2021, 44% in 2022, 35% in 2023), not as incidence per 1,000 births. No equivalent PPH incidence figure was located for Mae La. Reporting a "PPH rate comparison" would require inventing a denominator.

4. **The healthcare-delivery framing in the task does not match the 2017–2023 record.** Mae La's maternal care in this period was **not** delivered through Thai Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) integration. It was NGO-delivered — SMRU (Shoklo Malaria Research Unit, a Wellcome Trust/Mahidol-Oxford research unit) as sole provider of antenatal care (ANC) and delivery since 1997, with IRC and Malteser International providing primary care — with **referral out** to Thai public hospitals. MoPH integration in Mae La is a **2025 development** triggered by the collapse of US funding, not a 2017–2023 model.

5. **There was no discrete "2021 UNFPA funding reduction" affecting both locations.** UNFPA's Asia–Pacific expenditure *rose* by $30.3 million (18.1%) in 2021, explicitly attributed in part to scaled-up Cox's Bazar programming, and UNFPA signed a **$38.8 million** World Bank agreement for Cox's Bazar district in January 2021. The documented funding shocks are **2020 service consolidation**, **2023 (WFP ration cuts; HOPE Field Hospital CEmONC cessation)**, and **2025 (US aid suspension)**. Separately, UNFPA does not fund maternal health services in the Thai border camps at all, so a UNFPA funding shock cannot have had a Mae La effect.

---

## 2. Why three premises in the research brief required correction

# Medical-Grade Vaccine Refrigeration for 8 Rural MT/WY Clinics: Comparative Assessment
### Helmer GX Solutions vs. Thermo Fisher TSX Series vs. Panasonic/PHCbi MDF-DU702VH-PA

---

## 1. Executive Summary — Three Findings That Change the Procurement Question

**Finding 1 — The three products are not in the same equipment class.** The Panasonic/PHCbi **MDF-DU702VH-PA is a −86 °C ultra-low-temperature (ULT) freezer**, not a 2–8 °C vaccine refrigerator. PHCbi's own specification lists temperature control range −40 °C to −86 °C, effective capacity 729 L, two 750 W cascade compressors, and a 220 V NEMA 6-15P power supply ([PHCbi product page](https://www.phchd.com/us/biomedical/preservation/ultra-low-freezers/mdf-du702vhpa)). It cannot store routinely refrigerated vaccines, which CDC requires at **2 °C to 8 °C** ([CDC Toolkit](https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/hcp/downloads/storage-handling-toolkit.pdf)). The valid PHCbi comparator for this procurement is the **MPR Series** (2–23 °C, 5 °C factory preset) — but no evidence was found that any MPR model holds NSF/ANSI 456 certification, which is now a gating criterion (§6).

**Finding 2 — None of the three vendors powers refrigeration from an internal battery.** Every vendor battery in this comparison runs the *monitor, display, and alarms only*:
- Helmer i.Series: 20 h display & alarm backup, rechargeable 12 V lead-acid ([iPR125-GX data sheet](https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-02/iPR125GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380420-1.pdf)); Horizon Series only 2 h ([GX Freezer brochure, Oct 2024](https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2024-10/380477-1%20GX%20Freezer%20-30C%20Brochure%20Oct2024.pdf)).
- Thermo TSX: an internal CR123A/IEC16340 cell for monitoring only — the manual states plainly: *"This battery will not power the refrigeration. You must ensure uninterrupted power to the refrigerator and monitoring system"* ([TSX user manual](https://www.terrauniversal.com/media/asset-library/t/s/tsx-series-high-performance-undercounter-refrigerators-manual-thermo-fisher-scientific.pdf)). Thermo directs users to an external UPS for power and calls UPS "short-term."
- PHCbi: an alarm battery plus an optional **liquid-CO₂ back-up cooling kit (MDF-UB7-PW)** that the manual says prevents chamber temperature rise "for a few hours" ([MDF-DU502VH/702VH manual, §Back-up cooling kit](https://www.easymanua.ls/phcbi/mdf-du502vh/manual?p=56)).

**Consequence:** the 6–12 hour requirement is a **site infrastructure specification** (UPS sizing, generator, or both), not a product selection criterion. This should be procured and quoted separately, then validated during factory acceptance testing.

**Finding 3 — NSF/ANSI 456 certification is the strongest available proxy for what you actually care about.** NSF 456 tests cabinets with aluminum vaccine-simulation devices (VSDs) across 15 positions in three horizontal planes, applies consecutive 8-second door openings plus a 3-minute extended opening, and requires refrigerators to recover to **5 °C ±3 °C within 15 minutes** without any probe dropping below 1 °C or above 8 °C ([NSF white paper](https://documents.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LPD/Technical-Notes/Vaccine%20Storage%20Standards%20by%20NSF%20International%20Whitepaper.pdf); [Lab Supply Network summary](https://labsup.net/blogs/blog/nsf-ansi-456-for-vaccine-storage)). Helmer GX and Thermo TSX/TSG are documented as NSF 456 certified; PHCbi MPR is documented only as "CDC compliant," which is a marketing term, not a certification.

---

## 2. Corrected Product Matrix

| Criterion | Helmer GX (i.Series iPR113/120/125-GX) | Thermo TSX Series (e.g., TSX2305P*) | PHCbi MDF-DU702VH-PA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product class | 2–10 °C pharmacy/vaccine refrigerator | 2–8 °C (setpoint 3–7 °C) pharmacy refrigerator | −40 to −86 °C ULT freezer |
| CDC temperature band | Refrigerated (2–8 °C) ✔ | Refrigerated (2–8 °C) ✔ |

# Who Designed Longwood Gardens' 2008 "Nature's Castles" Treehouses — and Where the Contemporaneous Record Lives

## Bottom line

"Nature's Castles: The Treehouse Reimagined" was not the work of a single architect. It was a collaboration among **two specialist treehouse design-build firms** plus a **local architect of record**:

| Treehouse | Designer / builder | Contemporaneous attribution |
|---|---|---|
| **Canopy Cathedral** (near the Italian Water Garden / Large Lake) | **Peter Nelson (with Jake Jacob/Jacobs), TreeHouse Workshop, Inc., Seattle, WA** | Daily Local, 4/24/2008; Delaware Today, 8/2008; Main Line Today, 8/27/2008; The Reporter, 4/24/2008 |
| **The Birdhouse** (Terrace Woodland, near the Peirce-du Pont House) | **TreeHouse Workshop, Inc. (Peter Nelson), Seattle, WA** | The Reporter, 4/24/2008; Lancaster Online, 4/24/2008 |
| **Lookout Loft** (Forest Walk, behind the Peirce House) | **Forever Young Treehouses, Burlington, VT** (co-founded by **Bill Allen** and **Phil Trabulsy/Trabulsky**) | Daily Local, 4/24/2008; Delco Times, 4/24/2008; Delaware Today, 8/2008 |
| **All three** (coordination, code compliance) | **Matthew Millan / Matthew Millan Architects**, Philadelphia — explicitly called **"the architect of record"** | Washington Post, 10/2/2008 |

The best single contemporaneous source for **design concept *and* construction process** is **The Reporter Online (Lansdale, PA), April 24, 2008** — <https://www.thereporteronline.com/2008/04/24/the-skys-the-limit-at-treehouse-exhibit/> — supplemented by **Jane Holahan's Lancaster Online piece of the same date** and the **Philadelphia Inquirer's May 16, 2008** accessibility feature.

---

## 1. The event and its dates

- The exhibit was part of Longwood's **Arbor Day weekend** programming, opening to the public **Friday, April 25, 2008** (the Inquirer's preview is dated April 25; the Philadelphia Inquirer's May 16 piece says it "opened April 26"; the Daily Local preview ran April 24). Everyday admission was $16 adults / $14 seniors / $6 students 5–22 / free under 4. — <https://www.inquirer.com/philly/phillywomen/20080425_Open_house_-_up_in_the_Longwood_trees.html>
- Billed run: **through November 23, 2008**. — <https://www.thereporteronline.com/2008/04/24/the-skys-the-limit-at-treehouse-exhibit/>
- It was **"two years in the making"**; the **Canopy Cathedral's design began in February 2007**, when the designer first scouted the site **during a snowstorm**. Actual construction took about **four months**. — Lancaster Online, 4/24/2008 (<https://lancasteronline.com/features/entertainment/treehouses-get-the-longwood-gardens-treatment/article_b9546a06-8269-50ca-bb93-dbd4c0feb118.html>); Main Line Today, 8/27/2008 (<https://mainlinetoday.com/life-style/lofty-digs/>)
- Cost: **roughly $1 million**, reportedly "as much as traditional homes." — Inquirer, 5/16/2008 (<https://www.inquirer.com/philly/entertainment/20080516_Lofty_ideas.html>); Main Line Today, 8/27/2008

## 2. The design concept

- **Programmatic intent.** Longwood Director **Paul Redman**: *"Nature's Castles is designed to celebrate trees and engage our guests in an exciting and unique way about the beauty and importance of trees."* The treehouses were sited to draw visitors into **less-frequented groves of old tulip poplars** on the former du Pont estate — a deliberate tie to Pierre du Pont's 1906 purchase of Peirce's Woods, made specifically to save the trees from the sawmill. — Daily Local, 4/24/2008 (<https://www.dailylocal.com/2008/04/24/longwood-builds-natures-castles-in-the-gardens-trees/>); Delaware Today, 8/11/2008 (<https://delawaretoday.com/uncategorized/theres-nothing-lovely-as-a-tree/>)
- **Three distinct, complementary concepts** rather than one repeated form:
  - *Canopy Cathedral* — an ornate, two-story **Norwegian stave-church**–inspired timber-frame structure with an intricate glass façade, "hand-carved fantastical creatures throughout," a 118 sq ft balcony, and a large "prow" window. — Daily Local 4/24/2008; The Reporter 4/24/2008; Lancaster Online 4/24/2008; Millan Architects portfolio (<https://millanarchitects.com/portfolio/institutional/natures-castles-the-treehouses-at-longwood-gardens-the-canopy-cathedral/>)
  - *The Birdhouse* — the **smallest but tallest** house, 20+ ft up, giving a "true bird's eye / squirrel's-eye view"; built over a large rotted-out trunk left in place so visitors could look inside it, and detailed with a copper cable rigged as a **lightning rod** and a barn door with a rhododendron-branch handle. Longwood's current site notes the design drew on **steel forest-fire lookout towers**, with a wide staircase winding around a tulip poplar trunk. — Daily Local 4/24/2008; The Reporter 4/24/2008; <https://millanarchitects.com/portfolio/institutional/natures-castles-the-treehouses-at-longwood-gardens-the-birdhouse/>
  - *Lookout Loft* — a rustic **Adirondack-style** structure of two linked viewing platforms (one roofed, one trellised), designed to be **universally accessible**; Forever Young's stated mission is "to have entirely accessible treehouses in every state." Its ornate handrail was inspired by the **Gothic Folly in Longwood's recently opened Indoor Children's Garden**. — Daily Local 4/24/2008; Delco Times 4/24/2008 (<https://www.delcotimes.com/2008/04/24/treehouses-are-looking-up-at-longwood-gardens/>); Lancaster Online 4/24/2008
- **Interpretive layer.** Visitors could dial in a **cell-phone audio tour** of the three houses, and designers held "Meet the Treehouse Designers" sessions the opening weekend (11 a.m.–2 p.m.) alongside arborist demonstrations and tree-climbing gear demos. — Lancaster Online 4/24/2008; Inquirer 4/25/2008
- **Documentary.** A **documentary on the building of "Nature's Castles" aired on NBC-10 at 7 p.m., April 28, 2008**. — The Reporter, 4/24/2008
- **Public lecture by the designers.** An April 21, 2008 event listing, *"Treehouses: the Nuts & Bolts & What Holds Them Up,"* is billed as: *"Peter Nelson, Jake Jacobs and Matthew Millan of the Treehouse Workshop discuss topics such as tree selection, construction specifics and the building process."* — <https://archive.upcoming.org/event/treehouses-the-nuts-bolts-what-holds-them-up-427292>

## 3. The construction process

The single richest contemporaneous description of construction methodology is The Reporter (4/24/2008), corroborated by the Daily Local and Lancaster Online:

- **"Pin foundation," not tree attachment.** *"Instead of bolting the treehouse structures to the trees, or pouring a concrete foundation, all three treehouses are supported by sets of five-foot steel pipes, making up a 'pin foundation' which doesn't disturb the root systems."* The Daily Local elaborates: concrete footings with **extended steel rods threaded between tree roots** "and cause no damage." — The Reporter; Daily Local; also summarized by Penn State's PA Book heritage article (<https://pabook.libraries.psu.edu/literary-cultural-heritage-map-pa/feature-articles/longwood-gardens-preservation-paradise>)
- **Structural steel engineering.** The Canopy Cathedral alone used **37 steel columns, 34 steel beams and eight steel braces**. The Lookout Loft is held up by **13,000 lb of salvaged steel**. — Lancaster Online; Daily Local
- **Loading design (the key quantitative engineering fact).** *"The architect of record, Matthew Millan, worked with engineers to make sure that the structures met building codes, including that they could take 'live loads' (engineer speak for human beings) of 100 pounds per square foot, 2 1/2 times the code requirement for private homes."* — Washington Post, 10/2/2008 (<https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/2008/10/02/artisan-treehouses-extend-their-lease-at-longwood-gardens/0872cd19-1d4a-445c-a2f0-d7206d80de84/>)

  *Arithmetic:* implied private-residential code basis = 100 ÷ 2.5 = **40 psf live load**; the treehouses were engineered at **250%** of that.
- **Sustainability as a design constraint.** Redman: "environmental responsibility in the design of the treehouses was important… Each of the treehouses contains some degree of recycled, reclaimed, salvaged or sustainably harvested wood." Specifics:
  - Canopy Cathedral floors/beams: **Douglas fir salvaged from an old toothpaste factory in Toronto**, plus timbers milled from **logs recovered from a 2002 wildfire in Oregon**; cedar shakes/planking. — Lancaster Online; Delaware Today; Daily Local
  - Birdhouse: **salvaged wood from an old dairy barn**. — Daily Local
  - Lookout Loft ramps/handrails: **hop-hornbeam from Vermont and ipe** (a Brazilian hardwood) shaped like tree limbs, combined with wrought iron, finished with a **natural citrus-oil-and-beeswax** finish. — Lancaster Online; Daily Local
  - The large "prow window" was fabricated by **Scheel & Sharp of Norristown, PA**. — The Reporter
- **Accessibility engineering.** Forever Young installed **more than 75 feet of ramps** leading to three platforms up to **14 feet** off the ground, designed to ADA standards. Spokeswoman Patricia Evans: *"It's a joy to see kids in wheelchairs, who have never been in a treehouse, wheeling around up there."* — Lancaster Online; Delaware Today; Main Line Today
- **Lead builder.** Lookout Loft's lead builder was **Erych Stauffer** of Forever Young; Bill Allen: *"These trees have been waiting for a treehouse for 100 years."* — The Reporter

## 4. How permanent? (a construction question answered in real time)

The exhibit was marketed as seasonal, but the construction was permanent. Lancaster Online: **"the three treehouses were built as permanent structures."** Daily Local quoted Redman that duration was undetermined but they **"definitely would not be torn down in November."** By October 2008 the Washington Post reported the dismantling plan was abandoned and they would remain **"possibly five years."** Longwood's current site records that they **"were meant to live through Labor Day of the year they were constructed, but they proved so popular they remain here today."** — Lancaster Online 4/24/2008; Daily Local 4/24/2008; Washington Post 10/2/2008; <https://longwoodgardens.org/gardens/lakes-district/large-small-lake>

## 5. Reconciling the two attributions (designer vs. architect of record)

There is a genuine, resolvable tension in the record:

- **2008 press coverage credits the treehouse specialists as designers.** Daily Local: Canopy Cathedral "Designed by Peter Nelson and Jake Jacob of Treehouse Workshop Inc in Seattle"; Lookout Loft "Designed by Forever Young Treehouses of Burlington, Vt." Delaware Today / Main Line Today: the Birdhouse and Canopy Cathedral are "the work of Peter Nelson and Jake Jacobs of TreeHouse Workshop in Seattle." The Reporter: "The design by Peter Nelson of TreeHouse Workshop in Seattle." Daily local coverage of Lookout Loft: "designed by Forever Young Treehouses of Burlington, Vermont, co-founded by Bill Allen and Phil Trabulsy."
- **Millan Architects' own portfolio claims a broader design role**: the firm "worked with Longwood Gardens and the two premier treehouse companies in the U.S. to create these unique arboreal structures" and "designed each of the treehouses to respond to their individual settings and offer different interpretive opportunities." — <https://millanarchitects.com/portfolio/institutional/natures-castles-the-treehouses-at-longwood-gardens-the-lookout-loft/> and sibling pages
- **The 2008 Washington Post reconciles them explicitly**: Matthew Millan is **"the architect of record"** who worked with engineers on code compliance and live loads. The Upcoming.org listing likewise has Millan alongside Nelson and Jacobs presenting on "the Treehouse Workshop" and the building process.

**Most defensible synthesis:** the originating *treehouse design concepts* were Peter Nelson/Jake Jacobs (TreeHouse Workshop, Seattle) for the Canopy Cathedral and Birdhouse, and Bill Allen/Phil Trabulsy (Forever Young Treehouses, Burlington) for the Lookout Loft; **Matthew Millan (Millan Architects, Philadelphia) served as architect of record**, coordinating documentation, engineering and code compliance across all three.

final.content:
# Progressive Disclosure vs. Persistent Navigation in ERP Interfaces for Mid-Sized Manufacturers Migrating from AS/400

## Scope, method, and evidence-quality note

This report synthesizes peer-reviewed HCI/IS research, official vendor documentation (SAP, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft), change-management research (Prosci, 1,618 respondents), and vendor/integrator case studies. Evidence quality varies sharply and I flag it throughout. Three tiers:

- **Tier A (peer-reviewed, controlled):** NN/g studies, ACM/ICEIS papers, QUT aging studies, IS journal experiments.
- **Tier B (vendor official documentation):** Microsoft Learn, Oracle NetSuite Help, SAP Fiori Design System, SAP Community release blogs.
- **Tier C (vendor/integrator marketing or single-case):** Ulises, ControlERP, CYB Software, Upscend, Epicor, ECOSIRE. Useful for direction, not for effect sizes.

**Critical caveat up front:** I found **no controlled study that directly measures training-time reduction attributable to progressive disclosure in an ERP**, and **no published AS/400→cloud migration that reports user proficiency, time-to-competency, or error-rate metrics for production supervisors.** Those are genuine gaps, not oversights. Claims below are extrapolated where necessary and labeled as such.

---

## 1. Core finding: progressive disclosure improves learnability and time; it does not reliably reduce errors by itself

The single most-cited source is Jakob Nielsen's NN/g article, which states progressive disclosure "improves 3 of usability's 5 components: learnability, efficiency of use, and error rate," and that hiding advanced settings "helps novice users avoid mistakes and saves them the time they would have spent contemplating features that they don't need" (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/progressive-disclosure/). Two design constraints are specified:

1. **The split must be right.** "You have to disclose everything that users frequently need up front... the initial display can't contain confusing features or you'll slow down user performance."
2. **The path forward must be obvious**, with strong information scent on the advanced-options control.

Nielsen also warns that **more than two disclosure levels typically have low usability** — users get lost moving between levels. This is directly relevant to ERP, where deep menu hierarchies are the status quo.

**However, the strongest ERP-specific experiment contradicts the "simplification reduces errors" reading.** Parks (2012, ACM) tested users completing an **inventory procedure** in PeopleSoft, comparing the multi-screen default interface against a simplified single-screen version, quantifying complexity with GOMS-KLM and a visual model. Findings:

- The default complex screens required **almost twice as many steps** to navigate and **seven times the number of on-screen elements**.
- **Complexity was a significant variable only for time spent on the task, not success.**
- Task success depended on whether each user **scanned and verified data before submitting** — an observed behavior, not an interface property.
(https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2380790.2380799)

**Implication for your workflow design:** simplification reliably cuts task time and training burden. It does **not** reliably eliminate errors. Error reduction in inventory/work-order workflows comes from designing *verification affordances* into the submission step, because that is where the observed success determinant lives. A "simplified" screen that removes the confirmation/verification step may increase errors even as it reduces completion time.

A second, weaker data point points the same direction on magnitude of gain: a 2026 pre-post study of an ERP interface redesign (205 paired evaluations, higher-education ERP — **not** manufacturing) found mean task completion time fell **364.84 s → 220.86 s** and error rates fell **74.6%**, while correlations between perceived usability and objective performance were only **weak to moderate** (https://exa.ai/library/publication/mrpv75k8h6q). The weak correlation matters: subjective "users like it" scores are not a proxy for measured task performance. **Do not accept user-satisfaction surveys as your proficiency evidence.**

---

## 2. Persistent navigation: the evidence is mixed, and complexity of the task is the moderator

The classic assumption that persistent navigation always beats hidden navigation is not cleanly supported in the academic literature:

- A 1999 Indiana University study placed 44 participants across **linear, persistent, and semi-persistent** menu structures. **No significant differences** were found in task success, completion time, satisfaction, or perceived usability (https://exa.ai/library/publication/g3ywsxwsrj5). Caveat: web-based information-finding, not application data entry.
- NN/g's own later study (179 users, 6 sites, desktop + mobile) found hidden navigation **decreased discoverability and findability**, increased interaction cost, and reduced the likelihood that navigation was used at all (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/find-navigation-desktop-not-hamburger/).

The reconciling evidence is the **task-complexity moderator**:

- A 2009 study comparing **expandable menus (full context preserved)** vs. **sequential menus (partial context)** found that for **highly complex retrieval tasks** (long path length, low path relevance), expandable menus were **more efficient** and users were **less disoriented**. Practical implication stated: "for complex websites path relevance and expandable navigation menus are important usability considerations" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/rkzk4l4vdyj).
- An IBM study of **secondary navigation in software wizards** (30 participants across 3 sites, tasks that are "complex and/or performed infrequently") found the **table-of-contents** control produced the highest success and preference, users **preferred having a secondary navigation control over none**, and they still relied on Back/Next for actual movement (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/632716.632896).

**Synthesis for your case:** Work order creation and inventory adjustments are exactly "complex and/or infrequent" tasks with long path lengths. The evidence favors **persistent, context-preserving navigation for the advanced path** (expandable sections, tabs, a visible anchor/TOC) rather than burying advanced functions behind deep disclosure. Progressive disclosure should govern *what is on the entry screen*, not *how discoverable the second level is*.

---

## 3. Age and cognitive load: the 45–60 cohort is understudied, but the adjacent evidence is consistent and counterintuitive

Your target cohort (45–60) sits between the working-age and the 65+ samples that dominate the aging-interface literature. Extrapolation is necessary and should be treated as directional.

**Directly relevant findings:**

- **QUT (Gudur, Blackler, Popovic & Mahar, 2011):** older people (65+) completed tasks **faster on a words-only interface than on a redundant text+symbols interface**; all other participants were **faster on the redundant interface**. The companion QUT paper adds: older people used all three interfaces more slowly and less intuitively than younger participants, but there were **no age differences in errors on the words-based interface**, and the authors explicitly conclude that "recommendations to use redundant interfaces for greater usability for older people may need to be re-visited" (https://eprints.qut.edu.au/46980/ ; https://eprints.qut.edu.au/197616/1/46736098.pdf).
  - **Design consequence:** icon-heavy, symbol-driven navigation — common in cloud ERP launchpads — may actively slow your 45–60 supervisors. Text labels with icons *optional* are the safer default.
- **ERP-induced stress (WI 2015, N=227 across two organizations):** usefulness, **complexity, reliability, and pace of change** are the ERP characteristics that generate stressors and exhaustion. The comparative analysis found **elderly ERP users perceive ERP characteristics more negatively and are more stressed and exhausted than younger users** (https://aisel.aisnet.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1092&context=wi2015 — abstract retrieved; full text was not retrievable in this session).
- **ERP usage and cognitive workload (NASA-TLX survey):** differences in perceived cognitive workload by **age and gender**; the paper cites Czaja & Sharit on aging and technology use, noting older adults "often face greater challenges in adapting to new technologies due to declines in cognitive and motor abilities" (https://www.healthinformaticsjournal.com/index.php/IJMI/article/download/1548/1433/2789).

**"Pace of change" is an actionable, under-discussed lever.** It appears in the stress model above alongside complexity. A migration that changes navigation, terminology, and process simultaneously loads all three stressor dimensions. Phased navigation changes (keep legacy vocabulary visible during transition) are a defensible mitigation even though I found no controlled test of it.

**Manufacturing-specific cognitive ergonomics is nascent.** A 2024 MDPI paper designs (but has not yet run) an experiment measuring shop-floor cognitive load on the **SAP standard Production Operator Desk** using heart rate, body temperature, skin conductance, and subjective self-assessment, with a Design-of-Experiments method (https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1702/12/3/195). A 2024 review of cognitive-load-reduction techniques for manufacturing operators asserts that excessive cognitive load produces "errors, fatigue, and diminished performance" and that operators are "particularly susceptible" — but offers a framework rather than new measurements (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/387501541). Treat the causal chain as plausible, not proven, for your population.

A Polish UEQ study of ERP operation-registration screens in manufacturing environments is useful for *what production users value*: **pragmatic dimensions (perspicuity, efficiency, dependability) rated favorably; hedonic dimensions (stimulation, novelty) rated neutral to negative** (https://ph.pollub.pl/index.php/acs/article/view/7625). Your supervisors want clarity, speed, and reliability — not novelty. A "delightful" comprehensive dashboard directly contradicts this.

---

## 4. Vendor comparison: SAP S/4HANA, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics 365

All three vendors have converged on **role-based entry points with configurable disclosure** for shop-floor and supervisory personas. They differ mainly in *how granular the configuration is* and *how the advanced path is exposed*.

### SAP S/4HANA (Fiori)

- **Design principles are literally "role-based, adaptive, simple, coherent, and delightful,"** delivered through the Fiori launchpad, where "the user's role determines which app tiles are shown." Spaces and pages structure apps per business role; the shell bar is **always visible** — a persistent-navigation element sitting above a role-scoped entry layer (https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-139/foundations/integration-and-services/sap-fiori-launchpad/launchpad ; https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-120/.../sap-fiori-launchpad-spaces).
- **Explicit anti-pattern guidance:** "Do not try to translate the legacy UIs 1:1 into SAP Fiori screens... the resulting design has no additional UX benefits and conflicts with the SAP Fiori design principles." Also: "Avoid fragmenting the user experience into too many atomic applications," which produces "an unclear information architecture and frustrating navigation" (https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-71/discover/sap-products/sap-s4hana-only/ux-role-guidance — content retrieved via search index; direct fetch failed).
- **The "pyramid approach"** maps a business role to task levels: Level 1 = launchpad home page (single point of entry); Level 2 = domain overview (overview page or list report). This is a formalized progressive-disclosure model at the architectural level.
- **Inventory / work order specifics:**
  - *Manage Process Orders* is documented as "designed, keeping the supervisor persona in mind" and a "one-stop shop" — analytical list page with worklist table (status, quantity, operation progress) drilling to a **single details page** holding master and transaction data together (https://community.sap.com/t5/enterprise-resource-planning-blog-posts-by-sap/one-stop-view-for-production-supervisor-manage-process-order/ba-p/13507308).
  - *Process Warehouse Tasks* "enhances the usability by **avoiding navigation between multiple apps**," allowing single or multiple task confirmation/cancellation from one screen (https://community.sap.com/t5/enterprise-resource-planning-blog-posts-by-sap/manufacturing-and-supply-chain-in-sap-s-4hana-cloud-2005/ba-p/13442023).
  - *Manage Work Centers* centralizes display, create, change, mass replace, usage check, and capacity maintenance in one app (https://community.sap.com/t5/enterprise-resource-planning-blog-posts-by-sap/manufacturing-in-sap-s-4hana-cloud-2202/ba-p/13539488).
  - SAP publishes a **"Feature Comparison for Confirming Production Order Operations"** table contrasting classic visually-harmonized apps with new Fiori apps — a migration aid for deciding when the new path is genuinely better (https://community.sap.com/t5/enterprise-resource-planning-blog-posts-by-sap/manufacturing-in-sap-s-4hana-cloud-2108/ba-p/13511930).
- **SAP applies explicit progressive disclosure levels (0–3) for AI explainability:** "Level 3 Presents detailed information... Users access this level by clicking the explanation provided as a link in Level 1" (https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-84/foundations/ai-and-joule-design/guidelines/explainable-ai). This is a working template for "advanced function on demand" in S/4HANA.

### Oracle NetSuite

- **Role architecture is restrictive by design.** The standard **Specialized User: Manufacturing Operator** role provides *restricted* access to Manufacturing Mobile and Advanced Manufacturing Tablet flows, with default permissions for assembly builds, work orders, work order completions, work order issues, and BOM inquiries. Critically: "**You can restrict permissions, but you can't add permissions or assign access levels higher than those available in the standard role**" (https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/article_0617113517.html). This is **architectural progressive disclosure of capability** — the occasional-advanced-function need is handled by role design, not by UI control.
- **Inventory / work order specifics:** *Manufacturing Scheduler Dashboard* presents work-order data by work center as a chart with **color-coded operation status**, a data grid with task bars, an operation-view filter with **default vs. custom views**, a **Work Center / Work Order work-view toggle**, Expand All/Collapse All, and Daily/Weekly/Monthly time periods (https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/section_0223104719.html). The Work Center ↔ Work Order toggle and Expand/Collapse controls are textbook progressive disclosure and context-preserving navigation in one widget.
- Role/permission requirements for the Manufacturing Scheduler are enumerated explicitly (Work Order View/Edit, Work Calendar View, Locations View, etc.), so advanced functions are gated at the permission layer (https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/section_0223104112.html).
- **Role-customized dashboard case (Tier C):** A mid-sized electronics manufacturer's planners had a dashboard showing production volume and inventory but **not** supplier lead times or component shortages. After redesign to include late POs by vendor, work orders missing components, and a supplier-reliability trend, **late shipments dropped 18% in two months** (https://cybsoftware.com/how-to-customize-netsuite-dashboards-for-every-role-in-your-manufacturing-business/). Single case, vendor-authored, no methodology — but it is the clearest available statement of the "wrong dashboard for the role is worse than no dashboard" failure mode. Note the redesign did not add *more* data; it added *the right* data and removed noise.

### Microsoft Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management

- **Production Floor Execution (PFE) is the most granular configuration model of the three.** It is explicitly "role-based," "optimized for touch interaction," with visual contrast meeting accessibility requirements for shop floor environments, and supports job bundling (starting multiple jobs in parallel) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/production-floor-execution-use).
- **Configuration is per-device, not per-user:** "You must set up the production floor execution interface for each device... Companies typically set up each device differently." Setup requires the *Shop floor supervisor* role (the only out-of-box role with the *Maintain time supervision* duty). **Job filters ensure "only relevant jobs show on the device"** (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/production-floor-execution-setup).
- **Literal progressive disclosure in tab design:** each configuration defines a **Main view** (Active jobs / All jobs / My jobs / My machine), an optional **Details view** ("If you select the blank value, there will be no detailed view in the tab"), and a curated **Primary toolbar** of selected actions (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/production-floor-execution-tabs). Workers sign in with badge ID/personnel number — no Supply Chain Management user account required (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/production-floor-execution-use).
- Microsoft's own framing: the interface "minimiz[es] training time" and "each user sees only the most relevant data and actions for their tasks" (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/guidance/techtalks/production-floor-execution-interface-refresher). Note this is a **claim**, not a measurement.
