final.reasoning:
The user wants a complete research report as plain text. I need to synthesize the evidence gathered across the searches and fetches. Let me organize the report around the key clinical questions:

1. The clinical situation: 68yo man, 4 ED visits over 6 weeks for lightheadedness/fatigue, each time negative troponins, discharged. Most recent: HR 52, BP 118/74, O2 sat 98%, ECG sinus rhythm, first-degree AV block PR 240ms, occasional dropped beats not captured on telemetry. Prior ECG 3 weeks ago PR 200ms. On metoprolol 50mg BID started 8 weeks ago for HTN after prior cardiologist retired. Cr 1.1, K 4.3, Mg 2.0, TSH 2.8. Cardiology 3-month wait; insurance requires PA for event monitors and denies Holter without documented arrhythmia. Lives alone, drives daily, no family nearby.

Key clinical/legal/coverage questions:
- What monitoring strategy and authorization pathway would capture intermittent high-grade block while maintaining safety until definitive evaluation?
- Which clinical thresholds should prompt immediate pacemaker consultation rather than outpatient workup?

Key evidence:

**2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline** ([https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000627](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000627), [https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.043](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.043), [https://www.acc.org/-/media/Non-Clinical/Files-PDFs-Excel-MS-Word-etc/Guidelines/2018/Guidelines%5FMade%5FSimple%5F2018%5FBradycardia.pdf](https://www.acc.org/-/media/Non-Clinical/Files-PDFs-Excel-MS-Word-etc/Guidelines/2018/Guidelines%5FMade%5FSimple%5F2018%5FBradycardia.pdf)):
- First-degree AV block = PR >200 ms, 1:1 conduction
- Mobitz type II = constant PR, periodic single nonconducted P wave
- High-grade/advanced AV block = ≥2 consecutive P waves not conducting
- Class I: permanent pacing regardless of symptoms for acquired Mobitz type II, high-grade, or third-degree AV block "not caused by reversible or physiologic causes"
- For all other AV block types (e.g., first-degree, type I second-degree), pacing only if symptoms correlate
- ECG monitoring Class I if nondiagnostic after initial evaluation
- Ambulatory ECG monitoring Class I in initial evaluation when symptoms suggest bradycardia/conduction disorder
- ICM Class IIa for infrequent symptoms (>30 days)
- Echocardiogram Class I for Mobitz II/high-grade/third-degree
- Table 4 lists beta-blockers as medications that can induce/exacerbate bradycardia or conduction disorders

**Framingham data** ([https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/184145](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/184145)):
- PR >200 ms: AF incidence 140/10,000 person-years vs 36; pacemaker implantation 59/10,000 py vs 6; mortality 334 vs 129 per 10,000 py
- Absolute risk increases: 1.04%/yr AF, 0.53%/yr pacemaker, 2.05%/yr mortality
- HR 1.12 per 20-ms increment in PR
- This patient went from 200 → 240 ms: 40 ms increase → 1.12^2 ≈ 1.25 adjusted hazard for outcomes

**2017 Syncope Guideline** ([https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000498](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000498), [https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000499](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000499)):
- Class I: choice of monitor based on frequency/nature of syncope events
- Class IIa: Holter, transtelephonic monitor, external loop recorder, patch recorder, mobile cardiac outpatient telemetry useful
- External loop recorders with auto-trigger can capture asymptomatic arrhythmias; limited use in patients with sudden incapacitation
- Patch recorders 2-14 days
- MCOT with real-time transmission
- ILR for recurrent infrequent unexplained syncope

**2017 ISHNE-HRS consensus** ([https://www.heartrhythmjournal.com/article/S1547-5271(17)30415-0/fulltext](https://www.heartrhythmjournal.com/article/S1547-5271(17)30415-0/fulltext)):
- Prolonged monitoring has higher yield; SYNARR-Flash 4-week ELR high yield
- MCOT prospective RCT (Rothman et al, PubMed 17318994): MCOT made diagnosis in 88% vs 75% LOOP; clinically significant arrhythmias 41% vs 15%; for syncope/presyncope 89% vs 69%

**Metoprolol PI** ([https://labeling.pfizer.com/ShowLabeling.aspx?id=17205](https://labeling.pfizer.com/ShowLabeling.aspx?id=17205), [https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=cb76a73f-549a-4170-b96a-f93ed7e09464&type=display](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=cb76a73f-549a-4170-b96a-f93ed7e09464&type=display)):
- Contraindicated in significant first-degree heart block (PR ≥0.24 sec in MI context; generally stated as significant first-degree PR ≥0.24 s)
- "Patients with first-degree atrioventricular block, sinus node dysfunction, or conduction disorders may be at increased risk. Monitor heart rate and rhythm... If severe bradycardia develops, reduce or stop"
- PR 240 ms = 0.24 s is exactly the threshold in the PI for "significant first-degree heart block"
- Metoprolol slows AV nodal conduction
- This is a critical point: patient now has PR 240 ms while on metoprolol, which meets the PI threshold for "significant first-degree heart block" and the drug should be reconsidered/reduced

**Coverage pathways (CMS LCDs)**:
- NCD 20.15 ([https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/ncd.aspx?ncdid=179&ncdver=2](https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/ncd.aspx?ncdid=179&ncdver=2)): AECG covered for symptoms syncope, dizziness, chest pain, palpitations, SOB; ILR for syncope too infrequent for Holter/MLR
- LCD L39492 First Coast ([https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?lcdid=39492&ver=7](https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?lcdid=39492&ver=7)): AECG medically necessary for "unexplained syncope, near syncope, episodic dizziness" and "To assess documented or suspected bradycardia" — this is the key hook. The patient has documented bradycardia (HR 52) and first-degree AV block with dropped beats. The LCD explicitly covers "To assess documented or suspected bradycardia."
- LCD L40257 Palmetto ([https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?lcdId=40257&ver=7](https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?lcdId=40257&ver=7)): TNACMD reasonable/necessary when symptoms (dizziness, presyncope) occur infrequently (>24h between episodes); external loop recorders, patch recorders, MCT, MCOT; up to 30 days; auto-triggered devices capture asymptomatic events
- HealthHelp/AIM ILR policy ([https://www.healthhelp.com/wp-content/uploads/P_9852.pdf](https://www.healthhelp.com/wp-content/uploads/P_9852.pdf)): ILR appropriate if external monitoring non-diagnostic and symptoms infrequent
- BCBSTX policy ([https://medicalpolicy.bcbstx.com/content/dam/bbcs/medicalpolicy/pdf/medicine/MED202.003_2025-01-01.pdf](https://medicalpolicy.bcbstx.com/content/dam/bbcs/medicalpolicy/pdf/medicine/MED202.003_2025-01-01.pdf)): ILR after 14 days of noninvasive monitoring non-diagnostic
- Cigna policy ([https://static.cigna.com/assets/chcp/pdf/coveragePolicies/medical/mm_0547_coveragepositioncriteria_implantable_electrocardiographic_event_monitors.pdf](https://static.cigna.com/assets/chcp/pdf/coveragePolicies/medical/mm_0547_coveragepositioncriteria_implantable_electrocardiographic_event_monitors.pdf)): ILR medically necessary for recurrent/unexplained syncope after ≥14 days of noninvasive monitoring inconclusive

**Syncope driving recommendations** (2017 Syncope Guideline section 10.4, and 1996 AHA/NASPE statement [https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/01.CIR.94.5.1147](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/01.CIR.94.5.1147), [https://www.hrsonline.org/resource/1996-ahanaspe-personal-and-public-safety-issues-related-arrhythmias-may-affect-consciousness/](https://www.hrsonline.org/resource/1996-ahanaspe-personal-and-public-safety-issues-related-arrhythmias-may-affect-consciousness/)):
- Patients with arrhythmias that may impair consciousness should not drive until symptoms controlled

**2021 ESC pacing guidelines** ([https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/42/35/3427/6358547](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/42/35/3427/6358547), [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8785099/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8785099/)):
- Conservatively treated high-degree AVB worse survival vs paced
- ILR recommended for infrequent episodes (<1/month) if non-invasive testing non-diagnostic

Now the reasoning for monitoring strategy:

The patient has:
- 4 ED visits for lightheadedness/fatigue in 6 weeks
- Serial troponins negative (no ACS)
- ECG: first-degree AV block (PR 240 ms), occasional dropped beats not on telemetry
- Previous PR 200 ms → progression of 40 ms in 3 weeks
- HR 52 baseline
- On metoprolol 50 mg BID started 8 weeks ago — temporal correlation with symptom onset
- Metoprolol PI says PR ≥0.24 s is "significant first-degree heart block" — contraindication threshold; and patients with first-degree AV block at increased risk
- Dropped beats on ECG = second-degree AV block (though type not specified). If Mobitz II, that's a Class I pacing indication regardless of symptoms
- Dropped beats + first-degree block + PR prolongation suggests infranodal disease (especially if constant PR with non-conducted P waves = Mobitz II)
- The combination of first-degree AV block with intermittent non-conducted P waves and possible Mobitz II is concerning for progression to high-grade block
- "high-grade AV block" = ≥2 consecutive non-conducted P waves

Monitoring strategy:
1. Immediate: hold/reduce metoprolol (with BP monitoring) — PI explicitly warns; PR 240 = significant first-degree block threshold; this alone may resolve symptoms if drug-induced
2. ECG monitoring: The patient needs continuous auto-triggered monitoring with real-time or near-real-time transmission. Options:
   - External loop recorder (auto-triggered, weeks-months) — captures asymptomatic events
   - Mobile cardiac telemetry (MCOT) — real-time transmission, staffed 24/7 station; best for safety while living alone/driving
   - Patch recorder (14 days) — but shorter duration
   - Holter 24-48h — inadequate for intermittent symptoms every 6 weeks and insurance denies without documented arrhythmia (though the dropped beats now count as documented arrhythmia)
3. The key coverage hook: NCD 20.15 covers for dizziness/near syncope; LCD L39492 covers "documented or suspected bradycardia" — this is a slam-dunk since HR 52 and PR 240 and dropped beats are documented on ECG
4. If external monitoring captures high-grade/advanced AV block, Mobitz II, or symptomatic bradyarrhythmia → pacemaker consult/ER
5. If external monitoring non-diagnostic after 14-30 days, ILR (implantable loop recorder) is covered under NCD 20.15 and most commercial policies

Which thresholds prompt immediate pacemaker consultation rather than outpatient workup:
- Documented Mobitz II, high-grade (≥2 consecutive non-conducted P waves), or third-degree AV block — Class I pacing regardless of symptoms (2018 guideline)
- Symptomatic bradycardia with correlation (including symptomatic first-degree or type I second-degree — Class IIa/IIb territory)
- Syncope/presyncope with documented bradyarrhythmia
- Pauses ≥3 seconds (syncope guideline defines carotid sinus pause threshold; generally pauses ≥3 s while awake symptomatic are significant)
- Hemodynamic instability or concerning symptoms (falls, injury, syncope)
- The 2017 syncope guideline: hospital evaluation for patients with serious medical condition relevant to syncope cause
- Metoprolol PI: PR ≥0.24 s is a "significant first-degree heart block" and in the MI population is a contraindication; general PI says greater than first-degree block is contraindicated; patients with first-degree block at increased risk — should reduce/stop drug
- Since patient has HR 52 + PR 240 + dropped beats — this combination is near the threshold for inpatient telemetry and urgent EP evaluation. The dropped beats (second-degree AV block) with first-degree AV block suggests infranodal disease (Mobitz II pattern) and could progress. If the dropped beats are Mobitz II, that is already a Class I pacing indication regardless of symptoms (2018 bradycardia guideline).

Also: 2021 ESC guidelines note high-degree AVB untreated has notably poorer survival.

Safety while awaiting disposition:
- Driving restriction: AHA/NASPE 1996 statement recommends restriction for patients with arrhythmias that may impair consciousness; documented second-degree AV block + symptoms = should not drive until evaluated/paced
- Lives alone: MCOT with 24/7 attended surveillance is ideal because it can summon help

Insurance authorization pathway:
1. Cite NCD 20.15 and applicable LCD — symptoms of dizziness/near syncope plus documented bradycardia (HR 52, PR 240, dropped beats) are covered indications
2. If insurer denies Holter without documented arrhythmia: the dropped beats now ARE documented arrhythmia; use this as the medical necessity basis
3. Request external loop recorder or MCOT (auto-triggered) rather than patient-activated event monitor — critical because symptoms may cause incapacitation and patient may not trigger
4. If external monitoring non-diagnostic → ILR (implantable loop recorder) is the next step; NCD 20.15 explicitly states ILR is for syncope thought cardiac-related but too infrequent for Holter
5. Peer-to-peer with the LCD language: "To assess documented or suspected bradycardia" is sufficient
6. Expedited cardiology/EP consult: given PR progression 200→240 ms in 3 weeks, dropped beats, and 4 ED visits — request urgent/expedited referral; some EP groups have urgent access or the ED can arrange direct EP referral
7. Inpatient admission may be warranted: 2017 syncope guideline Class I hospitalization for serious medical condition potentially relevant to syncope cause; recurrent presyncope with documented second-degree AV block and PR prolongation may qualify; also the 2018 bradycardia guideline acute management pathway

Quantitative work:

If MCOT is unavailable, an auto-triggered ELR with daily remote transmission is the next best option; a patient-activated event recorder is insufficient for this patient.

- **ED return criteria**: Instruct the patient to return to the ED immediately for any syncope, fall, chest pain, dyspnea, resting HR <40 bpm, or worsening lightheadedness, rather than waiting for the scheduled follow-up.

- **Monitoring duration**: External monitoring should be continued for the full 30 days (or until a diagnostic rhythm is captured), since symptoms are every ~1.5 weeks and the first 7 days of monitoring are the highest-yield period but not sufficient to exclude events (Barrett et al., as summarized in LCD L39492; SYNNAR-Flash 4-week ELR data) (https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?lcdid=39492&ver=7; https://www.heartrhythmjournal.com/article/S1547-5271(17)30415-0/fulltext). If 30 days of external monitoring is non-diagnostic, proceed directly to ILR implantation under NCD 20.15 coverage.

## Summary of Recommended Actions

1. **Now**: Re-read the 12-lead ECG to classify the dropped beats (Mobitz I vs Mobitz II vs 2:1). If Mobitz II or 2:1 with constant PR: activate urgent EP/pacing consultation immediately — this is a Class I pacing indication and the 3-month waitlist is not acceptable. If the pattern is ambiguous, treat as high-risk and proceed as below.
2. **Now**: Have the managing physician reassess metoprolol — reduce or hold given PR 240 ms meeting the PI threshold for significant first-degree block, the temporal correlation with symptom onset, and resting HR 52. Substitute an alternative antihypertensive if needed.
3. **Same day**: Order an auto-triggered external loop recorder or MCOT (not Holter, not patient-activated event monitor). Cite NCD 20.15 (dizziness/syncope) and the applicable LCD ("documented or suspected bradycardia"). If denied, initiate peer-to-peer review using the guideline references above.
4. **Same day**: Advise the patient to stop driving until EP evaluation; document this. Establish a plan for a family/friend/neighbor check-in or a personal emergency response system given he lives alone.
5. **Within 1–2 weeks**: Complete the 30-day external monitoring. If it captures Mobitz II, high-grade block (≥2 consecutive blocked P waves), third-degree block, symptomatic bradyarrhythmia, or a symptomatic pause ≥3 s: immediate EP referral for pacemaker. If non-diagnostic, escalate to ILR per NCD 20.15 and 2021 ESC recommendations.

final.content:
MEMORANDUM: BUYER'S "REJECTION" OF LEGAL-SIZE PAPER UNDER UCC ARTICLE 2 — SUMMARY JUDGMENT ANALYSIS

Question Presented

Whether Buyer, who received 500 reams of legal-size (8½"×14") paper instead of letter-size (8½"×11") paper, used 180 reams in its operations, printed its letterhead and logo on the remaining 320 reams, and only then demanded return of payment while refusing Vendor's offer to exchange "remaining stock," rightfully rejected the goods or must pay the contract price subject only to a damages claim, with Vendor's proposed cure being ineffective on summary judgment.

Governing Law

The transaction is a sale of goods, so UCC Article 2 governs. The relevant provisions are § 2-601 (perfect tender), § 2-602 (manner and effect of rejection), § 2-606 (what constitutes acceptance), § 2-607 (effect of acceptance), § 2-608 (revocation), § 2-508 (cure), and § 2-714 (damages for accepted nonconforming goods). All citations are to the uniform text as enacted in the relevant state; the analysis is identical across UCC jurisdictions.

1. The Goods Were Nonconforming, But the "Standard Office Paper" Language Creates Some Ambiguity

The October 15 purchase order specified letter size. Under UCC § 2-313, a description of the goods ("letter size") becomes part of the bargain, and delivery of legal-size paper is a failure to conform. However, the contract also describes the goods as "standard office paper" without defining dimensions. "Standard office paper" in the United States customarily means letter size (8½"×11"), but legal size (8½"×14") is also a "standard" office paper dimension used in legal filings. See In re Amendment to the Florida Rules of Judicial Administration, 550 So. 2d 457 (Fla. 1989) (noting the historic dual system of letter- and legal-size paper in American offices).

For purposes of the rejection analysis, this ambiguity cuts both ways: it supports Vendor's argument that it had reasonable grounds to believe legal-size paper would be acceptable, and it may require parol evidence. But the ambiguity does not dispose of the case, because the dispositive issue is not whether the goods were perfect — it is whether Buyer's conduct after delivery constituted acceptance. Even if the goods were nonconforming, Buyer's right to reject expired through its own conduct.

2. Buyer Accepted the Goods as a Matter of Law

Under UCC § 2-606(1), acceptance occurs when the buyer: (a) after a reasonable opportunity to inspect, signifies acceptance; (b) fails to make an effective rejection under § 2-602 after having had a reasonable opportunity to inspect; or (c) does any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership. All three paths lead to acceptance on these facts, and the third is dispositive.

a. Use of the 180 Reams and Branding of the 320 Reams Are Acts Inconsistent with the Seller's Ownership (§ 2-606(1)(c))

The undisputed facts show Buyer:
- Used 180 of 500 reams (36%) for internal drafts and overflow projects over the three weeks following delivery;
- Printed the company's standard letterhead and logo on the remaining 320 of 500 reams (64%);
- Made no complaint to Vendor until November 30 — 22 days after delivery, after 100% of the goods had been consumed or irreversibly altered.

UCC Official Comment 4 to § 2-606 states that "any action taken by the buyer, which is inconsistent with his claim that he has rejected the goods, constitutes an acceptance." Consuming paper for ordinary business use and converting the rest into the buyer's own branded letterhead are quintessential acts of ownership. Courts have repeatedly so held: Lang v. Fleet, 36 Pa. D.&C.2d 361 (Phila. Mun. Ct. 1960) (buyer's use of a compressor to operate an air conditioner after a rescission demand was an "act inconsistent with the seller's ownership" and constituted acceptance); Cervitor Kitchens, Inc. v. Chapman, 82 Wash. 2d 673 (1973) (installation of goods into a building after opportunity to inspect is an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership, barring rescission); Sunkyong America, Inc. v. Beta Sound of Music Corp., 199 A.D.2d 100 (N.Y. App. Div. 1993) (resale of goods to retail customers constitutes acceptance under § 2-606(1)(c)). See also UCC § 2-606(2): acceptance of a part of any commercial unit is acceptance of that entire unit; here Buyer accepted all 500 units.

b. Buyer Failed to Make an Effective Rejection Within a Reasonable Time (§ 2-606(1)(b), § 2-602(1))

UCC § 2-602(1) requires that rejection occur "within a reasonable time after their delivery or tender" and be "ineffective unless the buyer seasonably notifies the seller." The paper-size defect was patent: it was apparent the moment any ream was opened or any sheet was fed into a printer, and employees complained about reformatting documents for three weeks. The office manager accepted delivery on November 8. Buyer first notified Vendor on November 30.

Whether rejection is timely is normally a question of fact, see Smith v. Paoli Popcorn Co., 255 Neb. 910, 587 N.W.2d 660 (1999) (Neb. UCC § 2-602 annotations), but where the undisputed facts show the buyer used or transformed the entire shipment before complaining, courts resolve the issue on summary judgment. See Knobel v. J. Bartel Co., 176 Wis. 393 (1922) (holding as a matter of law that a 25-day retention without notice, plus use inconsistent with the seller's ownership, constituted acceptance); Scott Anderson Trucking v. Nielson Construction Co., No. 20180274-CA (Utah Ct. App. 2020) (granting summary judgment for seller where buyer's 16-month delay before inspecting and rejecting was unreasonable as a matter of law under UCC § 70A-2-602; the court held the buyer breached by failing to timely inspect and reject); Miron v. Yonkers Raceway, Inc., 400 F.2d 112 (2d Cir. 1968) (buyer who fails to reject within a reasonable time after delivery with opportunity to inspect acts as an acceptor; on acceptance the buyer bears the burden of proving breach under § 2-607(4)). A 22-day delay alone might be factually disputable, but a 22-day delay during which Buyer consumed 36% and branded 64% of the goods is not. Acceptance under § 2-606(1)(b) and (c) is established.

c. The Office Manager's Acceptance of Delivery Does Not Equate to Acceptance Under § 2-606, But It Strengthens the Inference

Receipt of goods is not acceptance; acceptance requires a reasonable opportunity to inspect plus the buyer's manifestation of acceptance, failure to reject, or inconsistent act. The office manager's role is therefore not independently decisive. But it matters for another reason: the nonconformity was readily discoverable upon inspection, Buyer had a reasonable opportunity to inspect, and Buyer nonetheless proceeded to use all 500 reams. The office manager's acceptance of the shipment without verifying the specification does not excuse the buyer's subsequent consumption and alteration. Cf. Import Traders, Inc. v. Frederick Mfg. Corp., 117 Misc. 2d 305 (N.Y. Civ. Ct. 1983) (buyer's five-month silence after delivery constituted acceptance; UCC Comment 1 to § 2-606: acceptance occurs "by words, action, or silence when it is time to speak").

3. Effect of Acceptance: Buyer Must Pay, and Its November 30 Demand Was Not a Rightful Rejection

UCC § 2-607(1) provides that "the buyer must pay at the contract rate for any goods accepted." Section 2-607(2) provides that acceptance "precludes rejection of the goods accepted." Once acceptance occurred — by November 30 at the latest, and in fact progressively during the three weeks of use — Buyer's demand for return of payment was not a rightful rejection; it was a wrongful attempt to escape payment after exercising dominion over the goods. See Cissell Mfg. Co. v. Park, 36 P.3d 85 (Colo. App. 2001) (partial summary judgment for seller proper where buyer accepted and used dryers and only later attempted rescission; buyer obligated to pay at contract rate under § 4-2-607).

Buyer's only avenues after acceptance are (i) revocation under § 2-608, or (ii) damages under § 2-714 for the nonconformity of accepted goods. Both fail or yield little here.

a. Revocation Under § 2-608 Fails

Revocation requires a nonconformity that "substantially impairs its value to him" (§ 2-608(1)), and requires that revocation occur "before any substantial change in condition of the goods which is not caused by their own defects" (§ 2-608(2)). Both elements are absent. Legal-size paper has equivalent market value to letter-size paper and serves the same core function — office copying and printing; Buyer cannot quantify any lost hours and admits it cannot prove damages. And the "substantial change in condition" is overwhelmingly present: Buyer printed its letterhead and logo on 320 reams, destroying their value as generic resaleable merchandise. That change was caused by Buyer, not by the defect. Even if Buyer's actions were somehow not a prior acceptance, the attempted revocation would fail. See C.A.I., Inc. v. Vitex Packaging Group, Inc., 2015 WL 4378529 (D. Mass. 2015) (substantial impairment is an objective, common-sense determination; a change in condition caused by the buyer bars revocation).

b. Buyer's Only Remedy Is Damages Under § 2-714, Which Are Likely Nominal

UCC § 2-714(1) allows a buyer who has accepted goods and given timely notice of breach to recover "the loss resulting in the ordinary course of events from the seller's breach as determined in any manner which is reasonable." Under § 2-714(2), the measure for breach of warranty is "the difference at the time and place of acceptance between the value of the goods accepted and the value they would have had if they had been as warranted." Because legal-size and letter-size reams sell for essentially the same price, Buyer's damages are likely nominal or zero. Buyer's claimed "wasted staff time" is both unquantified and speculative, and under § 2-607(4) Buyer bears the burden of establishing any breach with respect to goods accepted. A claim for consequential damages under § 2-715 requires proof, and Buyer has none. Thus, even if Buyer's notice of November 30 was seasonable under § 2-607(3)(a), the damages claim is weak.

4. Vendor's Cure Offer Does Not Change the Result

Vendor argues that its offer to exchange the "remaining stock" for letter-size paper within five business days was a timely cure under UCC § 2-508. This argument fails for three independent reasons.

First, § 2-508(1) permits cure only where a tender "is rejected" and the time for performance has not expired. No effective rejection occurred: Buyer used and transformed all the goods before complaining. Cure under § 2-508 is a response to rejection; it cannot undo an acceptance. Acceptance precludes rejection under § 2-607(2), and a seller has no duty to cure an accepted delivery.

Second, § 2-508(2) — the curative provision available after the contract time when the seller "had reasonable grounds to believe" the tender would be acceptable — is factually available at most for the underlying conformance question, not for the rejection question. T.W. Oil, Inc. v. Consolidated Edison Co., 57 N.Y.2d 574 (1982), holds that a seller acting in good faith and without knowledge of a defect may cure within a further reasonable time if it had a reasonable expectation that the original goods would be acceptable. The contract's "standard office paper" language could support Vendor's reasonable belief that legal-size was acceptable, so if the case were solely about cure after a rightful rejection, summary judgment would be improper on that issue. But the cure provision presupposes an effective rejection. Here there was none; Buyer accepted by conduct before any rejection.

Third, and independently, the cure offer was impossible to perform in any meaningful sense. "Remaining stock" could only mean the 320 reams not yet consumed, but those 320 reams were already printed with Buyer's letterhead and logo. Vendor could not "exchange" reams that Buyer had converted into its own branded stationery, and Buyer could not return them in a condition that preserved Vendor's resale value. This is not the situation in Wilson v. Scampoli, 228 A.2d 848 (D.C. 1967), where the buyer refused a seller's offer to repair a television set that the buyer had not used or altered. Here, the buyer's own extensive use made cure impossible, which is precisely why cure is unavailable as a shield against acceptance. The buyer who destroys the goods' returnability cannot invoke the seller's right to cure to escape its own liability for the price.

5. Vendor's Incomplete Delivery Records and Missing Packing Slips Do Not Create a Genuine Issue of Material Fact

Vendor's delivery records for the period are incomplete, with packing slips missing for four other accounts. This evidence is immaterial to the present dispute. It concerns other transactions, not the November 8 delivery. Buyer admits receiving 500 reams of legal-size paper; the nonconformity is not in dispute. At most, the missing records could be used at trial to impeach Vendor's general credibility or suggest sloppy recordkeeping, but credibility alone does not defeat summary judgment where the material facts — delivery, size, use, and timing — are undisputed. A party opposing summary judgment must identify specific admissible evidence creating a genuine dispute on a material element; evidence about unrelated transactions does not satisfy that burden.

6. Summary Judgment Posture

Two possible motions must be distinguished:

If Vendor moves for summary judgment for the contract price under § 2-709(1)(a): the motion should be granted. The undisputed facts establish acceptance under § 2-606(1)(b) and (c): Buyer had a reasonable opportunity to inspect, failed to reject within a reasonable time, consumed 36% of the goods, and transformed 64% into its branded stationery before giving any notice of nonconformity. Acceptance obligates payment at the contract rate under § 2-607(1), and acceptance precludes rejection under § 2-607(2). Buyer's November 30 demand was therefore a wrongful rejection, not a rightful one. Any genuine dispute about the meaning of "standard office paper" goes to whether Buyer has a damages offset under § 2-714, not to liability for the price.

If Buyer moves for summary judgment for restitution or a declaration of rightful rejection: the motion should be denied. Buyer cannot prevail because its rejection was untimely and its conduct — use of 180 reams and printing of letterhead/logo on 320 reams — constituted acceptance as a matter of law. No reasonable jury could find a rightful rejection where Buyer used or altered 100% of the goods before complaining and where the nonconformity was patent and immediately discoverable.

The intermediate possibility — denying both motions and sending the case to trial — is not warranted on the dispositive issue. While "reasonable time" for rejection is fact-sensitive in many cases, the facts here are one-sided: all goods were used or altered during the 22-day window, and the defect was obvious from the first use. Cases such as Knobel v. J. Bartel Co. and Scott Anderson Trucking demonstrate that courts will resolve the acceptance issue as a matter of law where the buyer's delay and use are undisputed. The only genuinely disputed issues — the meaning of "standard office paper" and the amount (if any) of Buyer's damages under § 2-714 — affect damages, not the right to reject or the obligation to pay.

Conclusion

Buyer did not rightfully reject the goods. By failing to reject within a reasonable time after a reasonable opportunity to inspect, and by using 180 reams and printing its letterhead on the remaining 320 reams before making any complaint, Buyer accepted the goods under UCC § 2-606(1)(b) and (c). Acceptance precludes rejection under § 2-607(2); Buyer must pay the contract price and is limited to whatever damages it can prove under § 2-714, which appear nominal given the equivalent value of legal- and letter-size paper and Buyer's inability to quantify its claimed losses. Vendor's exchange offer cannot rescue Buyer because § 2-508 cure operates only on a rejected tender, and no effective rejection occurred; moreover, Buyer's own conduct made cure impossible by consuming or altering all 500 reams. On a properly supported motion, Vendor is entitled to summary judgment for the contract price, subject only to Buyer's unquantified — and likely nominal — offset for the nonconformity.

final.reasoning:
The task is to produce a legal analysis applying UCC Article 2 acceptance and cure principles to the described facts, to determine whether Buyer rightfully rejected or must accept subject to Vendor's proposed cure, in the summary judgment posture.

Key facts:
- Nov 8, 2024: Vendor delivered 500 reams legal-size paper, but Oct 15 PO specified letter size. Contract says "standard office paper" without defining dimensions.
- Buyer's office manager accepted delivery and stored reams in supply closet.
- Over three weeks, staff used 180 reams for internal drafts and overflow projects; employees complained about reformatting.
- Buyer printed company standard letterhead and logo on remaining 320 reams.
- Nov 30: Buyer demanded return of payment and refused Vendor's offer to exchange remaining stock for letter size within five business days.
- Vendor's delivery records incomplete; packing slips missing for four other accounts.
- Buyer claims workflow disruption/wasted staff time but cannot quantify hours lost.
- Vendor argues legal-size has equivalent value and Buyer's extensive use constitutes acceptance.

Analysis framework:

1. Nonconformity. The PO specified letter size. Contract says "standard office paper" — ambiguity. Under UCC 2-313, express descriptions are part of the bargain; the purchase order specifying letter size is a description. Since PO says letter size, and delivered legal size, goods fail to conform. But there's ambiguity because the contract says "standard office paper." The trade meaning of "standard office paper" in the US is letter size (8.5x11); legal size is 8.5x14. But the PO defines letter size. So the goods are nonconforming.

2. Perfect tender rule (2-601): if goods fail in any respect to conform, buyer may reject the whole, accept whole, accept commercial units and reject rest.

3. Acceptance (2-606): 
(a) after reasonable opportunity to inspect, signifies acceptance;
(b) fails to make effective rejection within reasonable time (2-602) — acceptance;
(c) does any act inconsistent with seller's ownership.

Here: Buyer's office manager accepted delivery and stored the reams. Over three weeks, staff used 180 reams for internal drafts. Buyer printed letterhead/logo on remaining 320 reams. These are acts inconsistent with seller's ownership. Using the goods in business operations, consuming 180 reams, and printing company letterhead on the remaining 320 reams, are all classic acts of ownership.

Also under (b): Buyer had reasonable opportunity to inspect — nonconformity (paper size) is readily discoverable upon opening a ream; the office manager accepted on delivery without inspection, then used goods for three weeks before Nov 30 demand. Rejection after three weeks of use is not timely; the goods are non-perishable but the defect is patent and immediately discoverable. But the question is whether it's "reasonable time" as matter of law or fact.

4. Use after opportunity to inspect: 180 reams used for internal drafts — consumption is inconsistent with seller's ownership. Printing 320 reams with company letterhead/logo is even more drastic — converting goods for buyer's own branded use, destroying their resale value.

5. Cure: 2-508(1) applies if time for performance hasn't expired — the PO of Oct 15, delivery Nov 8; contract time presumably expired by Nov 30. 2-508(2): seller may cure where buyer rejects nonconforming tender and seller had reasonable grounds to believe it would be acceptable. Vendor could argue reasonable grounds — the contract said "standard office paper," and legal paper is arguably standard office paper; there may be a genuine dispute. Vendor's incomplete records could hurt credibility but aren't determinative.

The timing of the cure offer: Vendor offered to exchange remaining stock for letter size within five business days. But by that time, 180 reams used and 320 printed with letterhead/logo — remaining stock can't be returned in original condition. Cure by exchange is only possible for the 320 reams? Wait — the 320 reams were printed on (letterhead/logo applied), so those 320 are also converted — they can't be "exchanged" in the sense the vendor offered "remaining stock" exchange. Actually "remaining stock" might mean the 500 reams minus the 180 used = 320, but those 320 are now printed with Buyer's letterhead/logo — they are customized and not returnable in original condition. Actually re-read: "Buyer also printed the company’s standard letterhead and logo on the remaining 320 reams." So all 500 reams have been used or altered. The vendor's offer to exchange remaining stock (the 320) is problematic because those are no longer in original condition — buyer used them for its own branded printing. But wait — "printed letterhead and logo on the remaining 320 reams" means the buyer used those reams to print letterhead onto — i.e., ran them through a printer to produce company stationery. So all 500 reams have been consumed or transformed. Exchange of remaining stock is impossible because the stock is no longer in re-sellable condition — Vendor can't resell 320 reams that now bear Buyer's letterhead/logo.

Buyer refused vendor's offer to exchange remaining stock within five business days. Under UCC 2-508(2) and cases like T.W. Oil v. Consolidated Edison, seller who acts in good faith and without knowledge of defect may cure if seasonable notice and reasonable expectation of acceptability. T.W. Oil: seller can cure by money allowance or replacement, further reasonable time. But cure is premised on rejection and the seller's ability to substitute conforming tender. Cure cannot undo the buyer's use of the goods. The vendor could only exchange the 320 reams' physical paper? No — those are printed with buyer's stationery. The exchange offer would require buyer to return the 320 reams, but they are now customized with buyer's letterhead — the buyer destroyed their commercial value; vendor would receive worthless customized paper. The cure offer is not meaningful for the 180 used reams and arguably not for the 320 altered reams.

But — key issue: acceptance occurred before any rejection. Under 2-607(2), acceptance precludes rejection. If Buyer accepted (through use/consumption and failure to make timely effective rejection), then Buyer cannot reject; the only path is revocation under 2-608, which requires substantial impairment of value. Legal-size paper vs letter-size: Buyer claims workflow disruption, but cannot quantify. Vendor argues equivalent value. Substantial impairment is a high bar; paper size difference may cause inconvenience but legal paper has substantial value for the same purpose (copy paper). Also, revocation must occur "before any substantial change in condition of the goods which is not caused by their own defects" — 320 reams printed with letterhead is a substantial change in condition caused by buyer, not by the defect. So revocation fails.

6. Summary judgment posture: Buyer moves for summary judgment on rightful rejection/restitution; or Vendor moves for summary judgment for price. Issue: are there genuine issues of material fact?

Acceptance facts are largely undisputed: Buyer's office manager accepted delivery, stored goods, staff used 180 reams over three weeks, and Buyer printed letterhead/logo on 320 reams. These are objective acts. Whether those acts constitute "acceptance" is a legal conclusion. The reasonableness of the time for rejection is normally a question of fact, but where the undisputed facts show extensive use and consumption, courts can decide as a matter of law. For example, courts grant summary judgment where buyer used goods for months without objection. Here, 180 reams consumed and 320 reams converted to letterhead over three weeks; the defect was patent. That is sufficient for a court to hold acceptance as a matter of law, at least under 2-606(1)(c).

But there are facts favoring Buyer: Vendor's delivery records incomplete, packing slips missing — but these relate to other accounts and don't bear on the actual delivery here. Vendor's records' incompleteness could be used to attack credibility but doesn't create a genuine dispute on the issue of whether legal-size was delivered (that's admitted).

Whether Seller had "reasonable grounds to believe" the legal-size tender would be acceptable is fact-intensive; the contract ambiguity ("standard office paper") could support Vendor's reasonable belief. But since cure is only triggered by rejection, and Buyer accepted, cure provisions don't apply in the same way. Actually, under 2-508, cure applies "where any tender is rejected." Where the buyer accepts, there is no right to cure in the rejection sense; acceptance precludes rejection. The buyer's remedy shifts to damages under 2-714.

However, even if rejection were effective, Buyer's refusal of the vendor's cure offer matters. Wilson v. Scampoli: buyer who refuses seller's reasonable cure offer cannot obtain rescission; seller must be allowed to cure. But Scampoli involved a defective TV that was returned/not used; here buyer used/consumed all goods. The cure offer to exchange "remaining stock" is impossible or at least problematic.

Another argument: Did Buyer accept? The office manager accepted delivery — but acceptance under 2-606(1)(a) requires "after reasonable opportunity to inspect." If the office manager accepted without inspecting and the nonconformity wasn't obvious until a ream was opened, there might be a fact question. But the office manager accepted delivery and stored the reams — this is receipt, not necessarily acceptance. The key acceptance event is the use: 180 reams used over three weeks, and 320 reams printed with letterhead.

Use after opportunity to inspect: The buyer had possession; paper size is readily apparent when a ream is opened. Use of 180 reams for internal drafts over three weeks with complaints shows the buyer knew or should have known of the nonconformity but continued using. Continued use after discovering nonconformity is an act inconsistent with seller's ownership, especially with full knowledge.

Also under 2-602: rejection must be within a reasonable time and seasonable notice. Buyer first complained on Nov 30, 22 days after delivery. For a fungible, storable commodity like paper, 22 days without rejection while consuming 36% of it (180/500 = 36%) and altering 64% (320/500 = 64%) is unreasonable as a matter of law in most jurisdictions. Cases like Miron (horse not rejected within reasonable time; acceptance) and Knobel (25 days without notice acceptance as matter of law) support this.

Quantitative work:
- 180/500 = 36% consumed
- 320/500 = 64% altered with letterhead/logo
- 500/500 = 100% of goods used or transformed before any rejection notice on Nov 30.
- 22 days from Nov 8 delivery to Nov 30 rejection demand.
- Vendor offered exchange within 5 business days (approx Nov 30 + 5 = around Dec 6-7).

These numbers are simple. I'll include them.

Now, on summary judgment: The question is whether Buyer rightfully rejected or must accept subject to cure. My analysis:

1. Buyer did not rightfully reject. Buyer accepted the goods under 2-606(1)(b) and (c) by (i) failing to make an effective rejection within a reasonable time, and (ii) using/consuming/transforming all 500 reams — acts inconsistent with seller's ownership.

2. Because acceptance occurred, 2-607(1) requires payment at contract rate; 2-607(2) precludes rejection. The Nov 30 demand is at most an attempted revocation under 2-608, which fails because no substantial impairment (legal paper remains usable office paper, only a dimension difference; Buyer cannot quantify harm) and because the goods underwent a substantial change in condition by Buyer's own printing before any attempted revocation.

3. Cure under 2-508: The vendor's offer to exchange remaining stock within five business days is moot/precluded because Buyer's acts of acceptance preceded any effective rejection. Even if the tender were treated as rejected, under 2-508(2), Seller could invoke cure if it had reasonable grounds to believe the tender would be acceptable — the ambiguous contract phrase "standard office paper" and the roughly equivalent commercial value of legal-size paper may give Seller a triable fact issue on reasonable grounds; but the cure offer cannot restore the 180 consumed reams, and the 320 reams are no longer returnable in original condition because Buyer printed its letterhead/logo on them. A cure offer that cannot put the goods back in a returnable condition does not excuse the buyer's wrongful refusal... actually, the cure offer is for the "remaining stock" but those reams are now customized. So cure is not a viable remedy that saves Vendor's case fully for the price? Wait, Vendor wants the price. If Buyer accepted, Vendor is entitled to the price under 2-709(1)(a) regardless of cure. Summary judgment for Vendor on the price would be appropriate if acceptance is established as a matter of law.

But Vendor's incomplete delivery records/packing slips missing for four other accounts — this is a red herring for this transaction. It doesn't create a dispute about whether delivery here was legal-size; Buyer admits receiving legal-size. It might matter for any claim that Vendor habitually misdelivers, but that's not relevant to the legal analysis.

4. Summary judgment determination: Genuine issues of material fact? The core facts of Buyer's use are undisputed. The legal effect — acceptance — is a question of law that can be resolved on summary judgment. Whether the reasonableness of the pre-rejection delay is a question of fact is the main counterargument (e.g., Smith v. Paoli Popcorn, La Villa Fair). Courts hold reasonableness of rejection time is a question of fact, but where the buyer uses goods extensively after discovering the defect, acceptance can be found as a matter of law. Here: 100% of goods used or transformed, 22-day delay, patent defect. Several courts have held that use after discovery of nonconformity constitutes acceptance as a matter of law.

However, a cautious court might find a genuine dispute on whether the three-week period was a "reasonable time" to inspect and reject, especially given the contract ambiguity about paper dimensions and that the office manager accepted delivery. If there is ambiguity about what "standard office paper" means, parol evidence could be needed — but the PO specified letter size; delivery of legal size is a failure to conform. Still, the interpretation of "standard office paper" could be a fact question. But even if there's a fact question on conformance, the use/consumption resolves acceptance.

Let me structure the report:

I. Jurisdiction/Governing Law — UCC Article 2 applies (sale of goods, 500 reams; goods are movable). Cite 2-102.

II. Nonconformity — PO specified letter size; legal delivered. Contract says "standard office paper." Under 2-313, description ("letter size") in PO forms part of bargain. Unless trade usage/parol evidence redefines "standard office paper," legal size fails to conform. The perfect tender rule (2-601) would allow rejection of nonconforming tender if timely.

III. Acceptance:
A. 2-606(1)(a): office manager accepting delivery and storing — receipt, not necessarily acceptance. But continued retention.
B. 2-606(1)(b): failure to make effective rejection — rejection on Nov 30, 22 days after delivery; under 2-602, rejection must be within reasonable time and accompanied by seasonable notice. Defect was patent (paper size obvious on opening). Buyer did not merely inspect — it consumed and altered the goods. Three weeks for storable, non-perishable paper with a patent size defect is likely unreasonable as a matter of law; question-of-fact language in some cases but the use eliminates the dispute.
C. 2-606(1)(c): acts inconsistent with seller's ownership — use of 180 reams in business operations and printing letterhead on 320 reams. The buyer converted all 500 reams (36% consumed, 64% branded). This is the strongest ground. Cite official comment 4 (any action inconsistent with rejection claim constitutes acceptance). Cite cases: Lang v. Fleet (using compressor for air conditioner = acceptance), Cervitor Kitchens (installation = acceptance), Sunkyong (resale = acceptance), Can-Key Industries.

D. Acceptance of part of commercial unit = entire unit (2-606(2)). Here commercial unit = ream? Each ream is a commercial unit; even accepting part of a unit accepts the whole unit. Buyer used all 500 reams anyway.

IV. Effect of acceptance: 2-607(1) pay contract rate; 2-607(2) acceptance precludes rejection. Nov 30 demand = wrongful rejection / at most attempted revocation.

V. Revocation analysis (2-608): even if buyer's actions weren't acceptance, revocation requires substantial impairment. Legal paper: equivalent value, same basic function. Buyer cannot quantify harm. Also 2-608(2) requires revocation before substantial change in condition not caused by defect — printing letterhead on 320 reams is a substantial change caused by Buyer. Revocation fails.

VI. Cure (2-508):
- Under 2-508(1), cure applies to a rejected tender before contract time expires. Contract time had expired. Whether 2-508(2) applies: seller had reasonable grounds to believe the tender would be acceptable? The contract phrase "standard office paper" creates an arguable basis; a court might find a genuine issue of fact. But cure under 2-508(2) requires a rejected nonconforming tender. Since there was no effective rejection — the Buyer accepted — cure is not available in the rejection sense.
- Also, cure depends on the buyer's ability to return the goods. Vendor could substitute letter-size for returned legal-size, but 180 reams are gone and 320 reams are irreversibly branded with Buyer's letterhead. The cure offer was thus not a conforming tender capable of placing the parties in status quo.
- Even if Buyer had effectively rejected, cases like Wilson v. Scampoli and T.W. Oil hold a seller in good faith with reasonable grounds can cure — but those cases involved goods substantially unimpaired. Here the Buyer's own conduct made cure impossible.
- Buyer's refusal of the vendor's exchange offer: Because Buyer had already accepted, refusal doesn't restore rejection rights; but the refusal also supports that Buyer's rejection demand was a wrongful attempt to escape payment after having used the goods.

VII. Vendor's incomplete records / missing packing slips: Immaterial. They concern other accounts, not this delivery; Buyer admits receiving legal-size paper. Without admissible evidence linking the records to this transaction, they don't create a genuine issue of material fact. At most they affect credibility, which doesn't defeat summary judgment when the material facts are otherwise undisputed.

VIII. Damages if accepted: Buyer may still pursue damages under 2-714 for nonconformity (difference between value as warranted and as delivered, plus incidental/consequential). But Buyer cannot quantify lost hours; legal paper has roughly equivalent market value, so damages are likely nominal or zero. Buyer must pay contract price but may offset for any proven nonconformity damages. The burden is on Buyer under 2-607(4).

IX. Summary judgment conclusion:
- If Vendor moves for summary judgment for the price: Should be granted to the extent of the contract price because Buyer accepted under 2-606, precluding rejection (2-607). The undisputed facts — 100% use/transformation, 22-day delay — establish acceptance. Under 2-709, seller recovers price for accepted goods.
- If Buyer moves for summary judgment for restitution/rightful rejection: Should be denied because rejection was not rightful; acceptance precludes it.
- The cure question is largely moot because acceptance occurred before rejection. Even viewing facts most favorably to Buyer, no reasonable jury could find that consuming and transforming all goods before complaining is a rightful rejection.
- One wrinkle: whether "standard office paper" reasonably meant legal size could be a fact dispute on the underlying breach; but that affects damages, not the right to reject after use. If there is a genuine dispute on conformance, summary judgment on the contract/price might still be granted because acceptance is established regardless — acceptance of nonconforming goods still obligates payment at contract rate, subject to a damages offset. Even if the goods conformed (if "standard office paper" is ambiguous and legal is acceptable), then there is no breach at all; Buyer must pay. Either way, Buyer must pay; only the damages offset question remains.

So on summary judgment: Buyer cannot avoid payment. Buyer's rejection was wrongful; acceptance occurred. Vendor's cure offer does not change the result because cure is a remedy for rejection, and there was no effective rejection; and because Buyer's use made cure impossible. Buyer's only recourse is damages under 2-714, which are likely nominal because Buyer cannot quantify losses and legal paper has equivalent value.

But I should be careful: the analysis of whether cure applies and whether the buyer must "accept subject to cure." The question asks "whether Buyer rightfully rejected or must accept subject to Vendor's proposed cure on summary judgment." So the conclusion: Buyer did not rightfully reject; Buyer accepted by conduct; the cure offer is moot because it can't undo the buyer's use; on summary judgment, Vendor is entitled to the contract price, Buyer is limited to 2-714 damages for the nonconformity, which appear nominal. If there is any genuine issue of material fact, it relates to damages, not to liability for the price.

Let me also mention: the "substantial performance" point in the task — vendor argues legal-size paper has equivalent value. Under UCC, perfect tender (2-601) technically applies to rejection, but that's only if rejection is timely. Since the buyer used the goods, the substantial-performance/impairment standard doesn't rescue the buyer at the rejection stage; at the revocation stage, substantial impairment (2-608) is the standard and Buyer fails.

One more thing: the buyer's office manager accepted delivery. Under 2-606(1)(a), "after a reasonable opportunity to inspect the goods signifies to the seller that the goods are conforming or that he will take or retain them in spite of their non-conformity." The office manager accepting delivery and storing the reams is arguably "retaining them" — but the statutory language requires signifying to the seller. Better to rely on (b) and (c). Also mention: acceptance and payment are distinct; "delivery" acceptance by receiving isn't necessarily acceptance under UCC.

Also mention UCC 1-204/2-103 reasonable time; the standard is commercial reasonableness.

Let me write the final report in a structured format, with inline citations to the source URLs I gathered:
- Cornell 2-606, 2-607, 2-602, 2-601, 2-508, 2-714
- Nebraska legislature annotations (Smith v. Paoli Popcorn, Fabricators, Alliance Tractor)
- Miron v. Yonkers Raceway
- T.W. Oil v. Consolidated Edison
- Wilson v. Scampoli
- Can-Key Industries, Cervitor Kitchens, Lang v. Fleet, Sunkyong America
- Michigan Bar journal article on acceptance/rejection/revocation
- Cissell Manufacturing v. Park (summary judgment accepted goods)
- Knobel v. J. Bartel
- Scott Anderson Trucking v. Nielson (summary judgment for unreasonable rejection delay)

Now write the report, no tool calls. Ensure only the report text, no narration. The report should answer the specific question. I can add section headings, cite URLs inline. Show the simple arithmetic. State uncertainty.

Report length: detailed but not bloated. Let me draft.

# Do You Need the ER for This Crohn's Episode? Yes — Go Now

**Bottom line: This combination of symptoms meets multiple explicit emergency criteria for inflammatory bowel disease. You should go to the emergency department now, not attempt to manage this at home with clear liquids.** Here's the evidence-based breakdown.

---

## 1. Your symptoms independently meet published ER red flags

The Crohn's & Colitis Foundation is explicit: "If your symptoms become severe, such as having heavy bleeding, **severe stomach pain, ongoing vomiting**, a high fever, or **signs of dehydration**, contact your healthcare team right away or **seek emergency medical care**" (https://www.crohnscolitisfoundation.org/patientsandcaregivers/what-is-ibd/managing-flares). You have four of these simultaneously:

- **Severe, intolerable abdominal cramping** (doubled over). The Foundation's patient education lists "Abdominal pain that you cannot tolerate or is constant" as an immediate-evaluation criterion (https://www.crohnscolitisfoundation.org/sites/default/files/legacy/assets/pdfs/newly-diagnosed.pdf).
- **Persistent vomiting** — you've thrown up everything since yesterday morning. The Foundation lists "Severe difficulty eating or drinking, causing symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, or pain" as a reason to be evaluated immediately (same PDF above).
- **Signs of dehydration** — dry mouth plus lightheadedness when standing are classic dehydration red flags. The Foundation lists "dry mouth, extreme thirst, dizziness" as emergency-warning signs of dehydration (https://www.crohnscolitisfoundation.org/sites/default/files/legacy/assets/pdfs/newly-diagnosed.pdf). Other authoritative sources independently confirm that feeling "dizzy or lightheaded, or feel like you may faint" warrants immediate medical care, and a dry mouth plus inability to keep fluids down is a "call doctor now or seek immediate medical care" criterion (https://www.commonspirit.org/conditions-treatments/dehydration; https://healthy.kaiserpermanente.org/health-wellness/health-encyclopedia/he.dehydration-care-instructions.tw12478).

---

## 2. A known stricture changes the risk calculus

Your scope six months ago showed narrowing — this is the single most important piece of context. Bowel obstruction is the **most common complication** of Crohn's disease (https://www.healthcentral.com/condition/crohns-disease/intestinal-blockage), and strictures are a leading cause: "Obstruction from stricturing Crohn's disease remains one of the most common reasons for intervention" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8292001/).

Mayo Clinic lists Crohn's strictures as a direct cause of intestinal obstruction, and says plainly: "seek immediate medical care if you have **severe abdominal pain** or other symptoms of intestinal obstruction" — whose symptoms include crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, and inability to pass stool or gas (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/intestinal-obstruction/symptoms-causes/syc-20351460). The American Gastroenterological Association's inpatient guidance is even more direct: "Prompt hospitalization should be considered for adult patients with IBD who present with severe disease refractory to outpatient treatment **when there is high suspicion for an IBD-related complication, such as intestinal obstruction**" (https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/inpatient-management-of-adults-with-ibd/).

The pattern you describe — known narrowing + intense cramping + vomiting everything — is the classic presentation of an acute obstruction in a Crohn's patient: "Patients with strictures often present to urgent care with acute obstructive symptoms of abdominal pain, distension and vomiting" (https://fg.bmj.com/content/13/6/524). The WSES-AAST emergency guidelines confirm intestinal obstruction is one of the "acute surgical emergencies" requiring emergency evaluation in IBD (https://wjes.biomedcentral.com/counter/pdf/10.1186/s13017-021-00362-3.pdf).

---

## 3. Why "ride it out at home with clear liquids" is not a safe option

The critical flaw in the home plan is that **you cannot keep liquids down**. Clear liquids only help if they stay in your body — and you've vomited everything since yesterday morning. That is precisely the threshold at which medical care is indicated:

- **You are at/past the 24-hour mark.** The NIDDK guidance, as widely cited, says adults should seek medical care if they cannot keep any fluids down for more than 24 hours, or develop signs of dehydration such as dizziness when standing, dry mouth, or not urinating for 6+ hours (https://www.solvhealth.com/health/diarrhea-vomiting-when-to-see-doctor). Vomiting since "yesterday morning" means you're already at or beyond that 24-hour window.
- **Gastroenterologist criteria for hospitalization in obstruction:** "The obstruction doesn't resolve within 24 hours; you can't tolerate liquids and are therefore at risk of dehydration; you have a lot of pain that you can't manage at home" — these three criteria are given by Arun Swaminath, MD, chief of gastroenterology at Northwell Lenox Hill (https://www.healthcentral.com/condition/crohns-disease/intestinal-blockage). You meet all three.
- **Hospital guidelines for stricture obstruction** say patients with suspected acute small bowel obstruction "should be initially kept nil per os (NPO) and hydrated adequately" — hydration in this state means IV fluids, not drinking (https://practicalgastro.com/2023/10/04/practical-approach-to-stricture-management-in-crohns-disease/).

Finally, the danger of waiting is not hypothetical. Mayo Clinic warns that untreated obstruction can cut off blood supply, causing the intestinal wall to die (necrosis), tear (perforation), and cause peritonitis (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/intestinal-obstruction/symptoms-causes/syc-20351460). Healthline notes a complete obstruction "can be fatal if not treated" (https://www.healthline.com/health/crohns-disease/intestinal-blockage). Delays in treatment for obstruction are associated with worse outcomes — surgical guidelines note "delays in operative treatment lead to increases in mortality and complications" (http://www.surgicalcriticalcare.net/Guidelines/SBO%202014.pdf).

---

## 4. What will happen at the hospital (so you know what to expect)

The good news: most obstructions do NOT require immediate surgery. The surgical-critical-care guidelines report 60–80% of small bowel obstructions respond to non-operative management, defined as (1) nasogastric tube decompression, (2) IV fluid resuscitation, (3) nothing by mouth, and (4) serial abdominal exams (http://www.surgicalcriticalcare.net/Guidelines/SBO%202014.pdf). MSD Manual similarly states: "Obstruction is managed initially with nasogastric suction and IV fluids. Obstruction due to uncomplicated Crohn disease should resolve within a few days" (https://www.msdmanuals.com/professional/gastrointestinal-disorders/inflammatory-bowel-disease-ibd/crohn-disease). MedlinePlus confirms partial obstruction without complications is managed with "bowel rest (nothing by mouth), intravenous (IV) fluids, and nasogastric (NG) tube decompression" (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000260.htm).

In the ER you can expect:
1. **IV fluids** to correct dehydration, and bloodwork for electrolytes (https://www.uhsussex.nhs.uk/resources/crohns-disease-obstructive-episode/; MedlinePlus above).
2. **A CT scan with IV contrast** — the WSES-AAST guidelines specifically recommend "IV contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan in the emergency setting" for suspected obstruction in IBD, and surgical guidelines make CT the standard for suspected small bowel obstruction (https://wjes.biomedcentral.com/counter/pdf/10.1186/s13017-021-00362-3.pdf; http://www.surgicalcriticalcare.net/Guidelines/SBO%202014.pdf).
3. **Possible nasogastric tube** to decompress the stomach and relieve vomiting (MedlinePlus above; https://practicalgastro.com/2023/10/04/practical-approach-to-stricture-management-in-crohns-disease/).
4. **Possible IV steroids** if imaging shows active inflammation in the stricture (AGA; https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/inpatient-management-of-adults-with-ibd/).

---

## 5. What to do right now

- **Do not eat or drink anything more** — you'll likely be kept NPO (nothing by mouth) anyway, and the NHS guidance for suspected obstruction is to stop eating and drinking for 3–6 hours while awaiting care (https://www.uhsussex.nhs.uk/resources/crohns-disease-obstructive-episode/).
