final.content:
# Autism Diagnostic Criteria in DSM-5 vs. ICD-11: Sensory Processing Differences and Clinical Implications

## A. Side-by-side criteria table

| Criterion row | **DSM-5 (APA, 2013)** | **ICD-11 (WHO, 2019)** |
|---|---|---|
| Core social-communication criterion | Three mandatory sub-criteria (all required): (A1) deficits in social-emotional reciprocity; (A2) deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction; (A3) deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships. Criteria may be met “currently or by history.” (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | One broad essential requirement: “persistent deficits in initiating and sustaining social communication and reciprocal social interactions that are outside the expected range of typical functioning based on the individual’s age and level of intellectual development.” Seven illustrative manifestations are listed (e.g., limitations in understanding/interest in verbal or nonverbal social communication, integration of spoken language with nonverbal cues, social awareness, ability to imagine and respond to others’ feelings, mutual sharing of interest, making/sustaining peer relationships) but no fixed number is required. (https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf) |
| Sensory processing mention/weighting | Sensory features appear as one of four equal sub-criteria under restricted/repetitive behavior (Criterion B): “Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement).” An individual must meet at least 2 of the 4 B sub-criteria, so sensory reactivity counts toward the threshold but is not independently necessary or sufficient. (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | Sensory features are explicitly included as one of seven listed manifestations of restricted, repetitive and inflexible behavior: “Lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli or unusual interest in a sensory stimulus, which may include actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures (especially clothing and food), odours and tastes, heat, cold or pain.” No minimum symptom count is specified — the ICD-11 requires only “a range of restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities that are clearly atypical or excessive for the individual’s age and sociocultural context.” (https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/) |
| Severity specifiers | Three mandated severity levels for both social communication and restricted/repetitive behavior: Level 1 “requiring support,” Level 2 “requiring substantial support,” Level 3 “requiring very substantial support,” each with behavioral anchors. (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | No severity levels analogous to DSM-5. Instead, ICD-11 uses subtype qualifiers based on two dimensions: disorder of intellectual development (present/absent) and functional language impairment, producing five profiles (e.g., 6A02.0 = ASD without disorder of intellectual development and with mild or no impairment of functional language; 6A02.1 = ASD with disorder of intellectual development and with mild or no impairment of functional language; etc.). (https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf; https://www.springermedizin.de/the-reclassification-of-neurodevelopmental-disorders-in-icd-11/51520996) |
| Age/onset requirement | “Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life).” (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | “The onset of the disorder occurs during the developmental period — typically in early childhood — but characteristic symptoms may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities.” DSM-5’s masking language is also present in substance: “Some individuals with autism spectrum disorder are able to function adequately in many contexts through exceptional effort, such that their deficits may not be apparent to others.” (https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/) |
| Functional impairment threshold | Criterion D: “Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning.” (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) | Requirement 4: “The symptoms result in significant impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning. Some individuals with autism spectrum disorder are able to function adequately in many contexts through exceptional effort, such that their deficits may not be apparent to others. A diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder is still appropriate in such cases.” (https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf) |

**Most important structural differences.** The DSM-5 uses a strict operational algorithm: all three A sub-criteria plus at least two of four B sub-criteria. ICD-11 uses prototype-based Essential Features: a global social-communication deficit plus “a range” of restricted/repetitive/inflexible patterns, with no minimum symptom counts in either domain (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825). The ICD-11 social-communication list explicitly includes items relevant to non-speaking and minimally verbal individuals, and the restricted/repetitive behavior list gives sensory reactivity equal status with routines, rituals, motor stereotypies and special interests. DSM-5 additionally provides a separate diagnosis, Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder, for individuals with social-communication deficits who do not meet the restricted/repetitive behavior threshold; ICD-11 has no direct analogue. (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml; https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825)

## B. Evidence synthesis: diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility studies

**1. Kulage, Smaldone & Cohn (2014). “How will DSM-5 affect autism diagnosis? A systematic literature review and meta-analysis.” Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 44(8):1918–1932.**
- **Design:** Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies identified from 418 records, comparing DSM-IV-TR vs. DSM-5 ASD criteria applied to the same populations.
- **Sample:** Aggregate across 14 studies (large pooled N); studies used ADOS, ADI-R, DSM-IV-TR/ICD-10 checklists and other instruments.
- **Key statistics:** Pooled decrease in ASD diagnosis under DSM-5 = 31% (95% CI 20–44%, p = 0.006); decrease for Autistic disorder = 22% (95% CI 16–29%, p < 0.001); decrease for PDD-NOS = 70% (95% CI 55–82%, p = 0.01); decrease for Asperger’s disorder = 70% but not statistically significant (95% CI 26–94%, p = 0.38). (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/)
- **GRADE quality:** *Low to moderate* (study-level risk of bias; diverse reference standards; direct comparison of criteria rather than clinical outcomes; consistent direction of effect).
- **Relevance to DSM-5 vs. ICD-11:** Directly quantifies the “under-diagnosis” risk that ICD-11 was designed to mitigate. Because the ICD-11 ASD category more closely follows a broad spectrum conceptualization without DSM-5’s strict 3-of-3 social requirement, many of the DSM-IV-TR-diagnosed individuals lost under DSM-5 would likely be retained under ICD-11 — an inference supported by the descriptive literature (https://europepmc.org/article/med/33269947), though not yet confirmed by head-to-head ICD-11 field data.

**2. First, Gaebel, Maj, et al. (2021). “An organization- and category-level comparison of diagnostic requirements for mental disorders in ICD-11 and DSM-5.” World Psychiatry, 20(1):34–51.**
- **Design:** Expert consensus comparison of the ICD-11 CDDG Essential Features vs. DSM-5 criteria for 103 diagnostic entities, with systematic ratings along a difference scale. Not a sensitivity/specificity study; it is the definitive published mapping of ICD-11/DSM-5 differences.
- **Sample:** 103 diagnostic categories rated by expert panels.
- **Key statistics:** 20 disorders (19.4%) rated “major differences,” 42 (40.8%) “minor definitional differences,” 10 (9.7%) “minor differences due to greater specification in DSM-5,” 31 (30.1%) “essentially identical.” For ASD specifically, the paper identifies the key definitional gap: DSM-5 requires all three social sub-criteria; ICD-11 lists seven illustrative manifestations without a minimum count. (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825; full text: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10119537/3/Brewin_First%20et%20al%20ICD-11%20DSM-5%20differences%20World%20Psychiatry%20final%20accepted%20version.pdf)
- **GRADE quality:** *Low* (expert narrative synthesis, no patient-level data, but high authority as the official harmonization-group output).
- **Relevance:** The paper explicitly notes the ICD-11 RRB examples are less dominated by features typical of individuals with both ASD and intellectual disability (e.g., object flipping, smelling/touching objects) and include sensory manifestations and special interests more characteristic of people without intellectual disability — a feature with direct implications for sensory-focused and previously-Asperger’s presentations. (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825)

**3. Wilson et al. / King’s College London adult clinic study (2013). “Comparison of ICD-10R, DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5 in an Adult Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Clinic.” Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 43:2515–2525.**
- **Design:** Primary empirical, cross-sectional diagnostic comparison in a clinical service.
- **Sample:** 150 intellectually able adults referred for autism assessment.
- **Key statistics:** Of adults diagnosed with ASD under ICD-10R, only 56% met DSM-5 ASD criteria; a further 19% met DSM-5 draft criteria for Social Communication Disorder. Of those diagnosed with Autistic Disorder/Asperger Syndrome under DSM-IV-TR, 78% met DSM-5 ASD criteria. Relaxing the DSM-5 criteria (reducing number of required items or rating “uncertain” items as “present”) significantly increased sensitivity without sacrificing specificity. (https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/; https://studyres.com/doc/8611005/comparison-of-icd-10r--dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult)
- **GRADE quality:** *Moderate* (single-site, moderate sample, but gold-standard instruments and direct diagnostic comparison; no ICD-11 arm).
- **Relevance:** Demonstrates that adults with Asperger-like presentations — a group whose diagnostic retention is a stated ICD-11 design goal — are precisely those most at risk of exclusion under DSM-5’s stricter algorithm.

**4. Beighley et al. (2013) and related DSM-IV-TR vs. DSM-5 sensitivity/specificity cohort evidence (Frazier et al., 2012; Huerta et al., 2012; McPartland et al., 2012).**
- **Design/primary empirical evidence:** Frazier et al. (2012) analyzed 14,744 siblings (8,911 ASD, 5,863 non-ASD) from the Interactive Autism Network; Huerta et al. (2012) applied DSM-5 criteria to 4,453 children with PDD diagnoses; McPartland et al. (2012) applied draft criteria to 933 individuals.
- **Key statistics:** Frazier et al.: DSM-5 specificity 0.97 vs. DSM-IV-TR 0.86; sensitivity 0.81 vs. 0.95; relaxing the algorithm to require one fewer criterion increased sensitivity to 0.93 with specificity 0.95. Huerta et al.: sensitivity of final DSM-5 criteria was 0.91–0.97 for children with DSM-IV PDD diagnoses. (https://scholars.mssm.edu/en/publications/an-organization-and-category-level-comparison-of-diagnostic-requi/; https://pure.johnshopkins.edu/en/publications/validation-of-proposed-dsm-5-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorde-6/; https://lirias.kuleuven.be/retrieve/288613)
- **GRADE quality:** *Moderate* (large samples, validated instruments, but draft criteria in some studies; no ICD-11 arm).
- **Relevance:** These studies establish the trade-off DSM-5 accepted — reduced sensitivity for higher specificity — which is the central safety concern when comparing DSM-5 with ICD-11’s intentionally broader, less prescriptive prototype.

**5. Vllasaliu et al. (2021)/“From pervasive developmental disorders in ICD-10 to Autism Spectrum Disorder in ICD-11” (Zeitschrift für Kinder- und Jugendpsychiatrie und Psychotherapie, 2020; PMID 33269947).**
- **Design:** Narrative review/expert clinical synthesis of ICD-10 → ICD-11 transition, with formal comparison to DSM-5.
- **Sample:** N/A (synthesis of published literature).
- **Key statistics:** Reports that ICD-11’s removal of “atypical autism” will likely decrease ICD-based prevalence relative to ICD-10, but that “sensitivity should remain high… and specificity may increase, similar to the changes that occurred going from DSM-IV-TR to DSM-5.” (https://europepmc.org/article/med/33269947)
- **GRADE quality:** *Low* (expert narrative, no systematic search).
- **Relevance:** One of the few peer-reviewed sources directly addressing diagnostic continuity between ICD-10 and ICD-11 for autism, and explicitly forecasting prevalence consolidation between ICD-11 and DSM-5.

**Evidence-synthesis summary.** No large, fully head-to-head randomized or prospective cohort study has yet compared DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 autism criteria applied independently to the same clinical population with blinded raters. The closest evidence is: (a) the ICD-11 developmental field study of mental disorder reliability (1,806 adults, kappas 0.45–0.88 across disorders; ASD not separately reported) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5980511/); and (b) the 2021 psychiatric services study of ICD-11 child/adolescent guidelines in Mexico City (52 children, kappas 0.46–0.53 excluding DBD) (https://www.psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.202000830). The default conclusion from the available literature is that ICD-11 will be at least as inclusive as DSM-5 for adults, women/girls, and cognitively able autistic people (because it lacks DSM-5’s 3-of-3 social requirement and explicitly acknowledges masking), but that this inclusiveness may come at the cost of lower specificity and higher false-positive risk (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/).

## C. Clinical guideline positions

**WHO.** The World Health Organization itself is the publisher of ICD-11. WHO’s stated position is that ICD-11 ASD requirements were “substantially updated to reflect the current literature, including presentations throughout the lifespan,” with qualifiers for intellectual functioning and functional language (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20611). WHO endorsed the inclusion of “atypical responses to sensory stimuli” as part of the ASD diagnostic requirements — a deliberate change from ICD-10 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/). WHO adopted ICD-11 at the World Health Assembly in May 2019, with WHO member-state reporting from January 1, 2022 (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20611).

**American Psychiatric Association (APA).** The APA published DSM-5 in 2013 and DSM-5-TR in 2022. The APA has not formally adopted ICD-11 for U.S. clinical diagnosis; DSM-5 remains the APA’s diagnostic standard, with ICD-10-CM codes used for U.S. billing. However, the APA’s DSM-5 Steering Committee has explicitly tasked itself with “harmonizing as much as possible with ICD-11” in future DSM revisions and has acknowledged that ICD-11 symptoms “are well aligned with the symptoms in DSM-5” (https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ajp.20250878). The APA’s DSM-5 criteria do not differentially weight sensory features beyond treating hyper-/hyporeactivity as one of four equal B sub-criteria (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml).

**American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).** No AAP policy statement formally adopting ICD-11 for autism was identified in the available evidence. The AAP continues to align clinical guidance with DSM-5 and with billing using ICD-10-CM. The AAP’s position is consistent with DSM-5’s functional-impairment requirement and its severity specifiers; the AAP has not issued a position on ICD-11 sensory weighting specifically.

**NICE (UK).** NICE explicitly endorses both systems. The current NICE autism guidelines (CG128 for under-19s; CG142 for adults) state that diagnosis should be made “based on ICD-11 or DSM-5 criteria” and that diagnostic assessment should focus on “developmental and behavioural features consistent with ICD-11 or DSM-5 criteria” (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/CG128/chapter/recommendations; https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg142/chapter/recommendations). Because the UK NHS officially uses ICD (the NHS has used ICD-10 and is preparing ICD-11), NICE’s practical diagnostic framework is ICD-anchored, with DSM-5 accepted as an alternative (https://www.patientlibrary.net/cgi-bin/download/file/239094). NICE’s context statement explicitly notes that in DSM-5, “restricted repetitive behaviours… interests and activities and sensory anomalies” form one of two required domains, acknowledging the sensory weighting in the criteria (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Context).

**Guideline-position synthesis.** WHO endorses ICD-11 as the global standard and explicitly includes sensory reactivity in the diagnostic requirements. NICE accepts both manuals and requires practitioners to use either “ICD-11 or DSM-5.” The APA maintains DSM-5 as its standard but has committed to future harmonization with ICD-11. AAP continues to operate within the DSM-5/ICD-10-CM framework. No major guideline body has recommended that sensory features be weighted more heavily than any other restricted/repetitive behavior criterion, though ICD-11’s no-minimum-count structure gives sensory features greater practical diagnostic reach relative to DSM-5’s 2-of-4 threshold.

## D. Advocacy organization positions on neurodiversity-affirming criteria

**Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN).** ASAN has repeatedly stated that autism diagnostic criteria must be broad enough to avoid excluding autistic people from access to accommodations. In its 2012 joint statement with the Autism Society of America, ASAN argued that the DSM-5 criteria “must be able to reflect that diversity and range of experience” and warned that narrowing the diagnosis undermines access to services; ASAN noted that “no publicly funded resource is accessible to autistic adults and children solely on the basis of a diagnosis,” arguing against excluding people to preserve resources (https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/01/joint-asan-autism-society-statement-on-dsm-5/). ASAN’s talking points specifically opposed the DSM-5 requirement that an individual meet 3 of 3 social communication sub-criteria, calling it “an overly restrictive standard” (https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/05/asan-talking-points-for-public-comment-on-dsm-5-autism-spectrum-disorder-criteria/). ASAN also opposed the DSM-5 severity scale (“we had… opposed the creation of both SCD and the severity scale”), arguing that severity based on “need for support” is preferable to deficit-based scaling, but that recording two separate severity levels still pathologizes autistic traits (https://www.thetransmitter.org/spectrum/will-new-dsm-5-autism-criteria-impact-services/). ASAN has no formal published position directly comparing DSM-5 vs. ICD-11, but its stated principles — no minimum item counts, recognition of masking, inclusion of the full spectrum, avoidance of deficit-based severity — align structurally more with ICD-11’s prototype-based, qualifier-based design than with DSM-5’s threshold algorithm. ASAN’s neurodiversity framework explicitly validates autistic people with or without a formal diagnosis and stresses that “there is no such thing as a ‘normal’ brain” (https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/what-we-believe/).

**National Autistic Society (NAS, UK).** The NAS is the largest UK autism charity. Its diagnostic guidance states that an autism diagnosis “should be based on criteria listed in the DSM-5 or the ICD-11, according to the NICE guidelines,” and notes that “both reference the ‘core characteristics’ of autism… including sensory differences.” The NAS describes restricted/repetitive behaviors as “often referred to by autistic people as self-soothing or self-regulating behaviours, and focused and dedicated interests,” explicitly reframing autistic traits in non-pathological, neurodiversity-affirming terms (https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment). Because the NHS uses ICD, the NAS effectively operates on ICD-11 in England. No NAS position statement was identified that declares one manual more neurodiversity-affirming than the other, but the NAS’s framing of sensory differences as a core, lifelong diagnostic feature reflects the ICD-11 wording (“lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity…”) more closely than DSM-5’s narrower “hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input” sub-criterion.

**Autism Speaks.** Autism Speaks’ DSM-5 FAQ describes the DSM-5 changes neutrally, emphasizing the consolidation of four DSM-IV categories into one ASD diagnosis and the clinician rating of severity by level of daily support (https://www.autismspeaks.org/dsm-5-and-autism-frequently-asked-questions). No formal Autism Speaks position statement on ICD-11 was identified in the available evidence. Autism Speaks is generally considered less aligned with neurodiversity positions than ASAN (ASAN has publicly criticized Autism Speaks’ framing and agenda), and Autism Speaks has not argued that ICD-11 is more neurodiversity-affirming. Its materials are primarily practical, focusing on service access and diagnostic consistency.

**Synthesis.** ASAN’s documented advocacy — for broad inclusive criteria, against 3-of-3 social requirements, against the SCD category, against two-part severity rating, and for recognition of masking — maps onto the structural differences that distinguish ICD-11 from DSM-5. NAS’s framing of sensory differences as integral to autistic experience likewise matches ICD-11’s more expansive sensory language. Autism Speaks has not taken a comparative position. Among the three, ASAN is the strongest voice for the view that ICD-11’s less restrictive, more experience-near criteria are more neurodiversity-affirming than DSM-5’s threshold-based algorithm; however, ASAN has not issued an explicit “ICD-11 is superior” statement, and the ICD-11 medical-model framing has itself been critiqued (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/).

## E. Diagnostic safety risks

**Under-diagnosis under DSM-5.** The strongest quantitative evidence concerns DSM-5’s risk of excluding people who would previously have received an autism diagnosis. Kulage et al.’s meta-analysis found a pooled 31% decrease in ASD diagnosis (range 7.3–68.4%) when DSM-5 was applied to DSM-IV-TR-diagnosed populations, with PDD-NOS showing the largest drop (70%) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/). Wilson et al. found that only 56% of ICD-10R-diagnosed adults met DSM-5 criteria, and warned that “reduced rates of ASD diagnosis may mean some ASD individuals will be unable to access clinical services” (https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/). Frazier et al.’s finding — DSM-5 sensitivity 0.81 vs. DSM-IV-TR 0.95, improving to 0.93 when one criterion is relaxed — confirms that the DSM-5 algorithm, not the underlying phenotype, drives the loss of diagnosis (https://pure.johnshopkins.edu/en/publications/validation-of-proposed-dsm-5-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorde-6/).

**Sensory-focused presentations and under-diagnosis.** Because DSM-5 requires at least 2 of 4 restricted/repetitive behavior sub-criteria, a sensory-focused adult with hyper-/hyporeactivity as their only RRB manifestation does not meet DSM-5 Criterion B. The same individual would likely meet ICD-11’s RRB requirement, since ICD-11 requires “a range” of restricted/repetitive/inflexible patterns without a minimum count, and sensory reactivity is listed among the seven examples. No direct study quantifying this specific scenario was identified, but the structural arithmetic is unambiguous: DSM-5’s B-criterion threshold is the binding constraint for sensory-dominant autistic adults (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml; https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf).

**Over-diagnosis/false-positive risk under ICD-11.** The principal safety risk on the ICD-11 side is decreased specificity. The critical-perspective article by a group of European researchers argues that ICD-11’s vague, non-falsifiable language “bears a large danger of false positive diagnoses, of further increased prevalence rates, limitations of access to ASD-specific services and of increasing the non-specificity of treatments,” and that ICD-11 may be difficult to differentiate from other mental disorders and “autism-like traits” (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/). This is a position paper, not an empirical study, and the concern is theoretical at this point because ICD-11 field testing has not yet produced ASD-specific sensitivity/specificity statistics.

**Inappropriate intervention risk.** The clearest intervention-safety link is mediated by service access: individuals who lose a DSM-5 ASD diagnosis may lose eligibility for autism-specific early intervention, behavioral supports, accommodations, and adult services; conversely, individuals who gain an ICD-11 diagnosis may gain access to the same services. Kulage et al. explicitly call for research on “policies regarding services for individuals lacking diagnosis but requiring assistance” (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/). No published study was identified that directly measured inappropriate treatment resulting specifically from DSM-5/ICD-11 differences.

**Risk summary.** DSM-5’s documented risk is *under-diagnosis* of cognitively able, sensory-focused, adult, and previously-PDD-NOS populations. ICD-11’s hypothesized risk is *over-diagnosis* and diagnostic non-specificity, with consequent service dilution. The sensory difference is one of the most plausible drivers of DSM-5-based under-diagnosis (because it is collapsed into a 2-of-4 RRB threshold) and one of the most plausible drivers of ICD-11-based inclusivity.

## F. Reimbursement and coding summary

**US (ICD-10-CM).** The United States uses ICD-10-CM for all HIPAA-covered billing transactions; ICD-11 has not been adopted for US morbidity/billing and CMS continues to require ICD-10-CM/PCS. NCVHS has recommended that HHS prepare for ICD-11 adoption, but a formal HIPAA rulemaking and implementation are projected no earlier than 2027–2029 (https://ncvhs.hhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Recommendation-Letter-Preparing-for-Adoption-of-ICD-11-as-a-Mandated-US-Health-Data-Standard-final.pdf; https://medsolercm.com/blog/icd-10-vs-icd-11-medical-billing-guide). The de facto US autism billing code is **F84.0 (Autistic disorder)**, which remains the standard code even though clinicians now diagnose “autism spectrum disorder” under DSM-5; the ICD-10-CM F84 block still contains DSM-IV-era subcategories (F84.0 Autistic disorder, F84.5 Asperger’s syndrome, F84.8 Other PDD, F84.9 PDD unspecified) (https://hccbuddy.com/icd10/F84.0; https://www.medcloudmd.com/post/icd-10-f84-0-autism-billing-documentation-guide-2026). This creates a well-recognized coding-diagnosis mismatch: a DSM-5 ASD diagnosis is routinely billed as F84.0 regardless of DSM-5 severity level or specifiers (https://www.medcloudmd.com/post/icd-10-f84-0-autism-billing-documentation-guide-2026).

**WHO crosswalk.** The official ICD-10 → ICD-11 mapping treats F84.0 as equivalent to **6A02.Z (Autism spectrum disorder, unspecified)** (https://autoicdapi.com/icd10-to-icd11/F84.0). This is a useful forward-mapping for future transition but has no current US billing effect.

**EU.** EU member states use ICD-10 (and nationally adapted ICD-10-GM in Germany, ICD-10-ES in Spain, etc.). WHO member states were asked to begin ICD-11 mortality/morbidity reporting from January 1, 2022, but implementation is asynchronous; the UK NHS, for example, has no confirmed ICD-11 mandate date (https://www.patientlibrary.net/cgi-bin/download/file/239094). In the UK, the NAS notes that NICE accepts either DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria; clinically, NHS England remains on ICD-10 coding pending transition planning (https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment; https://www.patientlibrary.net/cgi-bin/download/file/239094).

**Does adopting ICD-11 criteria affect coverage/reimbursement?** Adopting ICD-11 *diagnostic criteria* (what the clinician uses to decide whether the patient is autistic) does not by itself change reimbursement, because reimbursement follows the *billing code*, not the diagnostic manual. In the US, as long as ICD-10-CM is the HIPAA-mandated code set, a clinician can diagnose by DSM-5, ICD-11, or both and still bill F84.0. In the UK and EU, the same logic applies: the diagnostic criteria can be ICD-11-based while the statistical coding remains ICD-10 until national transition. However, there are indirect reimbursement effects: (1) if ICD-11 criteria are more inclusive, more people may receive an ASD diagnosis, generating more claims for autism-related services (ABA, speech therapy, occupational therapy); (2) if ICD-11 is more restrictive in some populations (e.g., removal of “atypical autism”), some previously diagnosable individuals may lose diagnostic eligibility and thus lose coverage in systems that require an autism diagnosis for service authorization; (3) the WHO 6A02.x subcodes allow more precise coding of intellectual/language profiles than F84.x, which could affect case-mix and risk-adjustment in future payment models (https://autoicdapi.com/icd10-to-icd11/F84.0; https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf).

**Bottom line.** Adoption of ICD-11 *criteria* can change who receives the diagnosis, thereby changing which patients generate autism-related claims, but it does not directly change the reimbursement code structure in the US (still ICD-10-CM F84.0). Full US adoption of ICD-11 for billing is likely still several years away; the NCVHS projected timeline places morbidity/billing implementation no earlier than 2027–2029 (https://ncvhs.hhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Recommendation-Letter-Preparing-for-Adoption-of-ICD-11-as-a-Mandated-US-Health-Data-Standard-final.pdf; https://medsolercm.com/blog/icd-10-vs-icd-11-medical-billing-guide).

## Overall conclusion

DSM-5 and ICD-11 agree on the two-domain structure of autism (social communication/interaction plus restricted/repetitive behavior) and on including sensory hyper-/hyporeactivity as a core diagnostic feature. The substantive differences are in *algorithmic strictness*: DSM-5 requires all three social sub-criteria and 2 of 4 RRB sub-criteria, with mandated severity levels; ICD-11 uses prototype descriptions with no minimum symptom counts, replaces severity levels with intellectual/language qualifiers, and gives sensory reactivity more expansive wording (“lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity… actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures… heat, cold or pain”). The evidence base shows DSM-5 reduces ASD diagnoses by roughly 31% relative to DSM-IV-TR/ICD-10 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/), with the greatest losses among cognitively able adults and PDD-NOS populations — precisely the groups whose inclusion the ICD-11 design was intended to protect. ICD-11’s inverse risk — false-positive diagnoses and reduced specificity — is a prominent concern in the literature but remains empirically unquantified (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/). For sensory-focused presentations specifically, ICD-11 is structurally more permissive: sensory reactivity counts toward the RRB domain without requiring a second RRB feature, whereas DSM-5 requires it to be accompanied by another B-criterion symptom. In terms of advocacy, ASAN and the NAS both emphasize inclusivity, masking recognition, and non-pathologizing descriptions of sensory and repetitive behavior, which aligns more naturally with ICD-11’s architecture, although neither organization has issued a formal head-to-head endorsement. From a reimbursement perspective, ICD-11 criteria can be adopted clinically without changing current billing, since US and EU payers still operate on ICD-10/ICD-10-CM codes, with the US transition projected no earlier than 2027–2029.

The single most important research gap is the absence of a large, blinded, head-to-head clinical validation study applying DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria to the same population — particularly one reporting sensitivity, specificity, and kappa for ASD across age, IQ, language, and sensory-dominant presentations. Until such a study exists, the comparative safety profile of the two manuals rests on inference from the DSM-5/DSM-IV transition literature and on the structural logic of the criteria themselves.

# Transitional Justice After Mass Atrocities: A Comparative Assessment of Truth Commissions, Prosecutorial Tribunals, Reparations, and Lustration

## 1. Framing the Question

"Transitional justice" (TJ) covers the measures a society adopts to reckon with legacies of gross human rights violations: criminal trials, truth commissions, reparations, lustration/vetting (screening public officials), amnesties, apologies, and memorialization. The field's central debate pits retributive mechanisms (prosecutions, lustration) against restorative ones (truth-telling, reparation), and pits "peace" against "justice" — the argument that pressing accountability can destabilize fragile transitions, versus the argument that impunity guarantees recurrence.

The evidence base is genuinely divided. A widely circulated survey, *The Effects of Transitional Justice Mechanisms*, concluded bluntly that "there is little evidence that TJ produces either beneficial or harmful effects," because rigorous cross-national analysis was scarce and the field was "driven by principles rather than data" (https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/103597/FullText.pdf). Later quantitative work is more optimistic but strongly conditional. The Transitional Justice Data Base (TJDB) found that TJ improves democracy and human rights scores — but only in specific *combinations*: trials plus amnesties, or trials plus amnesties plus truth commissions; truth commissions alone had a *negative* association with those goals (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:1875316a-4e73-436c-bf38-09c52943e66b/files/mb005fe06fd52177765574e6acba61df0; https://exa.ai/library/publication/yw3dwgxx98b). A Qualitative Comparative Analysis using the Post-Conflict Justice dataset similarly found that restorative measures, retributive measures, *and* amnesties can each contribute to durable peace, depending on the conflict and post-conflict context (https://ojs.lib.uwo.ca/index.php/tjreview/article/download/24047/18416/64314). A synthesis of 25 individual-level studies concluded that "transitional justice matters," that justice is understood by victims as a *social-political* rather than purely legal category, that different victims need different measures, and that outcomes depend heavily on context and implementation (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/pops.12395).

This report compares the four mechanism families using paired cases: South Africa's and Canada's truth commissions; the ICTY and the ICC's Kenya and Sudan cases; Germany's Holocaust reparations and the US Japanese American redress program; and post-communist lustration in Czechoslovakia/Czechia and East Germany. It then assesses which approaches best serve victims, enable democratic transitions, and prevent recurrence.

---

## 2. Truth Commissions

### 2.1 South Africa (1996–2003)

**Design.** The TRC was created by the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act (No. 34 of 1995) with three committees: Human Rights Violations (HRV), Amnesty, and Reparation & Rehabilitation (RRC). Its distinctive bargain was **conditional amnesty**: perpetrators could escape criminal and civil liability only by fully disclosing politically motivated gross violations. The Constitutional Court upheld this in *AZAPO v President* (1996), reasoning that amnesty was the "cornerstone" of the negotiated settlement *and* that the same act mandated reparations — "reparation is essential to counterbalance amnesty," because amnesty extinguishes victims' civil claims (https://sabctrc.saha.org.za/reports/volume5/chapter5/subsection0.htm; https://omalley.nelsonmandela.org/index.php/site/q/03lv02167/04lv02264/05lv02335/06lv02357/07lv02398/08lv02403.htm).

**Scale.**
- ~21,000–22,000 individual statements taken, describing violations affecting ~44,000 people (37,672 violations documented) (https://atjhub.csvr.org.za/south-africa-truth-and-reconciliation-commission-1996-2002/; https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Page-34-49.pdf).
- 7,112 amnesty applications; roughly 700–849 granted and ~5,392 refused (https://www.justice.gov.za/Trc/amntrans/index.htm).
- 21,676 people ultimately designated victims (https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Page-165-171.pdf).
- The TRC named ~17,000 victims, granted amnesty to nearly 700 perpetrators, and referred ~350 names to government for prosecution (https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Page-172-202.pdf).

**Reparations — the failure point.** The RRC recommended individual grants benchmarked to the 1997 median annual household income of R21,700, paid over six years, up to R23,023/year with dependants — implying roughly **R130,200–R138,000 per victim** (https://sabctrc.saha.org.za/reports/volume5/chapter5/subsection8.htm; https://sabctrc.saha.org.za/reports/volume6/section2/chapter1/subsection2.htm). Government delayed. Urgent interim reparations began only in 2003; 16,855 payments were made totaling R50 million (https://sabctrc.saha.org.za/reports/volume6/section2/chapter8/subsection7.htm). Parliament then approved a **one-off R30,000 grant** instead of the six-year scheme. Of 21,676 identified victims, 17,428 who applied were paid:

> R497,798,781 (final grants) ÷ 17,428 victims = **R28,563 per victim** — about **22% of the R130,200 recommended**.

Adding interim grants (R53,165,325), total disbursement was roughly R551 million (https://www.trc-inquiry.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Page-165-171.pdf). Thousands of eligible victims never received payment; over R1.43 billion sat unspent in the President's Fund as of 2018 (https://globalreparations.com/documents/Case_Study_-_South_Africa.pdf). The government also largely failed the TRC's "bold prosecutions" recommendation.

**Verdict.** The TRC is the gold standard for *truth-telling and victim voice* — it established an official, publicly owned record and forced apartheid's crimes into national consciousness. But its reparation and prosecution legs were largely unimplemented, and its amnesty extinguished civil claims without adequate compensation. This is the core cautionary lesson: a truth commission's value is bounded by what the political system does with its findings.

### 2.2 Canada (Truth and Reconciliation Commission on Residential Schools, 2008–2015)

**Design.** The TRC was one component of the court-supervised Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (IRSSA, 2006). It gathered testimony from more than 6,500 Survivors and released a Final Report and **94 Calls to Action** in 2015, concluding the residential school system constituted "cultural genocide" (https://reconciliation.ca/app/uploads/2026/07/2007-NCR-AR-2026_ENG_final.pdf).

**Truth vs. implementation.**
- **2023 (Yellowhead Institute):** zero Calls to Action completed; 81 of 94 unfulfilled (https://yellowheadinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/YI-TRC-C2A-2023-Special-Report-compressed.pdf).
- **2024:** one Call completed (CTA 53, via the National Council for Reconciliation Act, Bill C-29) (https://afn.bynder.com/asset/36043b91-4f8c-405e-8199-25c886017877/TRC-Report-Card-2024.pdf).
- **September 2025 (Assembly of First Nations):** approximately **13 of 94 completed**, with only two completed in the prior five years and none in 2024–25 (https://afn.bynder.com/m/21a223c344077b7/original/Progress-on-Realizing-the-Truth-and-Reconciliation-Commission-s-Calls-to-Action-September-2025.pdf).
- **10th anniversary (December 2025):** estimates of "fewer than 20" implemented, with one tally showing 14 completed, 42 in progress, 16 not started, 22 stalled (https://globalnews.ca/news/11579370/under-20-truth-and-reconciliation-calls-implemented-decade-later/; https://www.gx94radio.com/2025/09/29/trc-calls-to-action-10-years-later-progress-or-passivity/).

So after a decade, completion is in the **roughly 14–21% range** (13–20 of 94).

**Reparations — the counterpoint to South Africa.** The IRSSA created two compensation streams:

- **Common Experience Payment (CEP):** $1.9 billion fund; $10,000 for the first school year plus $3,000 per subsequent year. Total paid: **$1,622,422,106**, averaging **$20,457** per recipient; about 98% of the estimated 80,000 eligible former students were paid by December 2012 (https://www.cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1315320539682/1571590489978; https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/indian-residential-schools-settlement-agreement). Residual funds triggered non-cash "personal credits" up to $3,000 (https://residentialschoolsettlement.ca/IRS%20Settlement%20Agreement-%20ENGLISH.pdf).
- **Independent Assessment Process (IAP):** $5,000–$275,000 per person for proven sexual or serious physical abuse (https://www.residentialschoolsettlement.ca/detailed_notice.pdf).
- Plus $125 million to the Aboriginal Healing Foundation, $60 million for the TRC, and $20 million for commemoration.

**Verdict.** Canada shows a truth commission can be well-resourced and still founder on implementation of its forward-looking recommendations. It also demonstrates that *broad* compensation (a per-capita payment) is administratively achievable at scale, while *structural* reform (the Calls to Action) is where states stall. The 2024 establishment of an independent National Council for Reconciliation was a direct response to this accountability gap.

---

## 3. Prosecutorial Tribunals

### 3.1 ICTY (former Yugoslavia, 1993–2017)

**Output.** The ICTY indicted **161 individuals** over 24 years. Official figures: approximately **90–93 sentenced**, **18 acquitted**, **13 referred to national courts**, and ~37 proceedings terminated (deceased, withdrawn, or transferred) (https://www.icty.org/en/cases/key-figures-cases; https://www.icty.org/x/file/About/Infographics/Infographic_facts_figures_en.pdf). By ethnicity, indictees were overwhelmingly Serb (94 of 161), followed by Croats (29), Albanians (9), and Bosniaks (9); convictions roughly tracked this (62 Serbs, 18 Croats) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_indicted_in_the_ICTY). Slobodan Milošević died in 2006 before verdict; Ratko Mladić was sentenced to life in 2017.

**Sexual violence.** 78 indictees (48%) had sexual-violence charges; 32 were convicted for such crimes — a genuine legacy innovation in international law (https://www.icty.org/sid/10586).

**Cost.** Estimates cluster around **$2.3 billion** (through the assumed 2014 close) to **$2.7 billion** for the full 24-year life, with annual budgets exceeding $100 million (https://repository.law.uic.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1018&context=facpubs; https://repository.law.uic.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1501&context=facpubs). One comparative law study puts the average at roughly **$18 million per concluded trial** (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-journal-of-international-law/article/abs/costs-of-international-justice/C72C5059E6BF5F3ECDA217F1621777D1).

> **Worked comparison:** $2.5 billion ÷ ~90 sentenced ≈ **$28 million per person sentenced**.

**Contested legacy.** The 2012–13 acquittals of Ante Gotovina and Mladen Markač (Operation Storm, reversing 24- and 18-year sentences), plus Momčilo Perišić and the Stanišić/Simatović acquittals, produced a crisis of confidence. A sitting ICTY judge, Frederik Harhoff, circulated an email in June 2013 questioning the Tribunal's credibility and the dilution of "joint criminal enterprise" doctrine (https://www.toaep.org/pbs-pdf/49-slydal; https://www.cips-cepi.ca/2013/07/17/oversell-but-underperform-the-increasingly-troubled-legacy-of-the-icty/). The Gotovina Appeal Chamber itself split, with two judges dissenting (https://www.icty.org/en/sid/11145). Commentators argued the acquittal vindicated Croatian narratives and deepened Serbian victims' sense of injustice (https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/collapse-of-transitional-justice/). Defense counsel writing on the Tribunal's legacy described achievements as "impressive" but procedural and substantive justice as "uneven" (https://journals.uni-goettingen.de/gojil/article/download/2023/1717/4534). No government in the region conducted comprehensive truth-seeking, and surveys found publics viewed the ICTY as a foreign body rather than "their" tribunal (https://www.ictj.org/sites/default/files/ICTJ-FormerYugoslavia-Justice-Facts-2009-English.pdf; https://nsuworks.nova.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1315&context=ilsajournal).

**Verdict.** The ICTY established individual accountability and landmark jurisprudence (including for sexual violence), but its cost, duration, acquittals, and distance from affected societies limited its reconciliation impact. It functioned better as a fact-establishing and norm-creating institution than as a vehicle for victim redress or social repair.

### 3.2 ICC in Kenya

**Background.** After the 2007–08 post-election violence — the Waki Commission (CIPEV, 2008) recorded **1,133 deaths, 3,561 injuries, 117,216 instances of property destruction, and mass displacement**, with police responsible for all 405 recorded gunshot deaths (https://www.ictj.org/sites/default/files/ICTJ-Kenya-Dialogue-Inquiry-2008-English.pdf). Waki gave a sealed list of alleged perpetrators to Kofi Annan, who passed it to ICC Prosecutor Moreno-Ocampo in July 2009 after Kenya failed to establish a special tribunal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waki_Commission).

**Outcome.** Both flagship cases collapsed:
- **Kenyatta** (charges withdrawn December 2014): Prosecutor Bensouda cited Kenyan government non-compliance with evidence requests, witnesses who died or were "too terrified to testify," and key witnesses who recanted (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/statement-prosecutor-international-criminal-court-fatou-bensouda-withdrawal-charges-against-mr). The BBC called it "the most high-profile collapse of a case in the ICC's history" (https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-30353311).
- **Ruto and Sang** (charges vacated April 2016): 17 prosecution witnesses withdrew cooperation; the Chamber found the case "severely undermined by witness interference and politicisation," terminating it without prejudice to re-prosecution (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/ruto-and-sang-case-icc-trial-chamber-va-terminates-case-without-prejudice-re-prosecution; https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/statement-prosecutor-international-criminal-court-fatou-bensouda-regarding-trial-chambers).

**Domestic complement.** Kenya's own Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission delivered a 4-volume, 2,210-page report in May 2013 based on ~40,000 statements — but the National Assembly never adopted it or created the recommended implementation committee; the reparations framework was never enacted (https://www.hrw.org/news/2019/12/10/kenya-elusive-justice-gross-injustice-abuse; https://www.justiceinfo.net/en/44424-how-kenya-s-truth-commission-report-became-a-political-ghost.html).
